stories.title: India's forex reserves jump a record $10.5 billion in a week to $692.9 billion, as the RBI leans harder on NRI deposits to defend the rupee
stories.what_happened: RBI data released on Friday, August 7, showed India's foreign exchange reserves rose by $10.512 billion in the week ended July 31, taking the total to $692.866 billion — the sharpest one-week increase since the week ended January 30, and the highest reserve level in nearly three months. Foreign currency assets, the dollar, euro and other hard-currency holdings that make up the bulk of reserves, rose $8.75 billion to $564.68 billion, while gold reserves climbed $1.685 billion to $104.743 billion, reflecting both fresh accumulation and higher gold prices. Special Drawing Rights (a reserve asset allotted by the IMF) and India's reserve position with the IMF each ticked up slightly as well. Much of the jump traces back to the RBI's FCNR(B) swap scheme, through which Indian banks had pulled in $36.7 billion in NRI dollar deposits by July 31, drawn in by the RBI absorbing banks' currency-hedging costs so they can offer NRIs better returns than they'd get elsewhere. Analysts expect reserves to cross the $700 billion mark in the coming weeks if the pace of inflows holds, though some caution the rupee itself may see only limited relief from the buffer alone.
key_points: Reserves rose **$10.512 billion in a single week** (ended July 31) to **$692.866 billion** — the **biggest weekly jump since January 30** and a near-**three-month high**.
Most of the gain came from **foreign currency assets**, up **$8.75 billion to $564.68 billion**; **gold reserves** added another **$1.685 billion**, reaching **$104.743 billion**.

The surge is largely traced to Indian banks mobilising **$36.7 billion** through **FCNR(B) deposits** — a scheme that pays Non-Resident Indians attractive dollar-deposit rates, pulling those dollars into the country.
It comes as the **rupee** has fallen roughly **12% over the past year** and hit a **record low near ₹96/$** in May 2026, forcing the RBI to keep intervening to slow the slide.
Governor **Sanjay Malhotra** says reserves remain adequate by standard measures: over **10 months of import cover** and **90.8% external-debt cover**.

depth.background: Foreign exchange reserves are the stockpile of US dollars, gold, and other hard assets a country's central bank holds — used to pay for imports, service foreign debt, and step in to support the local currency when it's under pressure. India's rupee has been under sustained pressure through 2026 from global dollar strength and persistent capital outflows, and it touched a record low against the dollar in May. To defend the currency without simply burning through its existing dollar stockpile, the RBI has been running a scheme to pull in fresh foreign currency: a swap facility that makes it cheaper for banks to offer high-interest FCNR(B) deposit accounts to Non-Resident Indians, in exchange for their dollars flowing into India's reserves.

stories.title: Jharkhand's exam-scam protest escalates: a hunger striker is hospitalised as students prepare to gherao the state Assembly
stories.what_happened: The protest, which began around July 25-29, hit its 13th and 14th days on August 6 and 7 with the situation intensifying rather than cooling. Six protesters had been on hunger strike, and on August 7 one of them, Rahul Kranti — fasting since the night of August 4 — was rushed to Ranchi Sadar Hospital after his health worsened; Leader of Opposition Babulal Marandi visited him there. The same day, Chief Minister Hemant Soren publicly reached out to the agitating students for the first time, saying the government was ready for dialogue and committed to reforms, while Parliamentary Affairs Minister Radhakrishna Kishore announced a four-minister committee to monitor the protests. Students, in turn, finalised an 11-member delegation — eight student representatives, a lawyer and two technical experts — to negotiate with the government. Despite Jharkhand's CID arresting 11 people connected to the alleged leak, including a suspected 'mastermind,' protesters say they don't trust a state-run investigation and are holding firm on their demand for an outside CBI or retired-judges probe. With no resolution reached, students have announced they will gherao the Jharkhand Legislative Assembly on August 10 if their demands remain unmet.
key_points: The protest has entered its **14th day**, with student leader **Devendra Nath Mahto** on hunger strike since **August 3** demanding Chief Minister **Hemant Soren's** resignation.
Protester **Rahul Kranti** was **hospitalised on August 7** after his health deteriorated during the fast; five other students remain on hunger strike.
Students want the **14th JPSC exam** cancelled and re-held, plus an **independent CBI or judicial probe** — they've rejected the state's own **CID investigation** as untrustworthy.
Jharkhand's **CID** has already arrested **11 people**, including alleged 'mastermind' Suman Saurav, but that hasn't satisfied protesters.
Students plan to **gherao (surround and blockade) the state Assembly on August 10** if demands aren't met; CM Soren has now offered talks and formed a 4-minister panel to monitor the crisis.

depth.background: In July, aspirants preparing for Jharkhand's 14th Public Service Commission (JPSC) civil-services exam and the JSSC-CGL recruitment test alleged the papers had been leaked and results rigged, after screenshots of an answer sheet went viral appearing to show candidates who had failed still making the merit list. Under the banner of the 'JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch,' job aspirants began an indefinite sit-in at Ranchi's Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in late July. The movement has drawn direct inspiration from Delhi's recent 'Cockroach Janta Party' protests over the leaked NEET-UG medical entrance exam, which forced the Union Education Minister to resign — activist Sonam Wangchuk, who fasted 26 days over that issue, has personally called Jharkhand's hunger strikers. In a state where a government exam can be a once-in-a-generation shot at economic security, allegations that the process itself was rigged cut especially deep.

stories.title: Zelensky makes his first-ever visit to Serbia, meeting a Russia-friendly Vučić
stories.what_happened: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky traveled to Belgrade for an official visit on **August 8**, his first to Serbia since taking office. He is meeting Serbian President **Aleksandar Vučić** and Prime Minister Đuro Macut to discuss deepening economic ties, energy cooperation, and both countries' paths toward **European Union membership**. Vučić, asked whether the visit signals a shift in Serbia's stance on Russia, said Belgrade's sanctions policy was set **nearly five years ago** and will not change "for the foreseeable future." The visit comes as Zelensky continues a broader diplomatic push across Europe to keep allies engaged in Ukraine's defense and reconstruction planning.
key_points: Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Belgrade on **his first visit to Serbia** since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Serbia is one of the few European countries that has **refused to join Western sanctions on Russia**.
The two leaders are expected to discuss **EU integration, energy cooperation, and expanding trade ties**.
Serbian President **Aleksandar Vučić** said Serbia's sanctions policy, set nearly **five years ago**, will not change.

depth.background: Serbia has walked a careful line since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in **February 2022**: it has condemned the invasion at the UN but refused to impose sanctions on Moscow, partly because of deep historic, religious and economic ties to Russia. Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has cultivated relationships with both the West (Serbia is an EU candidate country) and Russia, buying time rather than picking a side. Zelensky, by contrast, has spent his presidency touring allied capitals to shore up military and financial support for Ukraine's defense. This trip is his **first as president to Belgrade**, a notable gesture toward a government that has stayed publicly neutral.

stories.title: Bus plunges 100 feet into a Himachal Pradesh gorge, killing at least 7
stories.what_happened: The bus was travelling from Bairagarh to Chamba town on Saturday morning when it skidded off the road near the Chalunj bend, overturned, and fell roughly 100 feet onto the road below. Local residents began rescue efforts before police and administrative teams arrived to take over. At least **7 people were killed** — including the bus driver and conductor — and **11 injured** people were taken to a hospital in nearby Tissa town. Officials have not yet determined the exact cause, and an investigation into the circumstances of the crash is underway.
key_points: A private passenger bus rolled off a hill road on the **Bairagarh–Chamba route** in Himachal Pradesh's Chamba district on Saturday morning.
It fell around **100 feet (roughly 30 metres)** into a gorge near the Chalunj bend after skidding off the road.
At least **7 people died**, including the driver and conductor, and **11 more were injured**.
Around **20–25 passengers**, mostly locals travelling to Chamba town, were on board at the time.

depth.background: Chamba is a remote, mountainous district in northern Himachal Pradesh where narrow, unpaved or poorly maintained roads wind along steep gorges — a common and recurring hazard across the Himalayan states. Overloaded private buses are the main form of public transport for people in these hill towns, since road infrastructure and traffic policing are thin. Fatal bus-into-gorge accidents are tragically frequent in Himachal Pradesh and neighbouring Uttarakhand, often blamed on a mix of bad roads, monsoon-weakened surfaces, and vehicle overcrowding.

stories.title: Amarnath Yatra suspended from Jammu as heavy rain and landslide risk shut down the route
stories.what_happened: Jammu and Kashmir authorities suspended the Amarnath Yatra from the Jammu side on Saturday, August 8, halting any new batch of pilgrims from leaving the Bhagwati Nagar base camp for the Kashmir Valley. The suspension follows a Meteorological Department forecast of heavy to very heavy rainfall across the Jammu region through August 11, alongside landslide risk on the Jammu-Srinagar national highway. Authorities said they are monitoring conditions and will decide on resuming pilgrim movement based on the weather and road conditions. More than 4.75 lakh pilgrims have visited the shrine since the Yatra began on July 3, and it is scheduled to run until August 28.
key_points: No fresh batch of pilgrims was allowed to leave Jammu's **Bhagwati Nagar base camp** on Saturday as authorities suspended the Yatra.
The Met Department has forecast **heavy to very heavy rain** across the Jammu region through **August 11**.
More than **4.75 lakh pilgrims** have already visited the cave shrine since the Yatra began on **July 3**.
The pilgrimage is due to conclude on **August 28**, Raksha Bandhan, unless further weather disruption pushes that back.

depth.background: The Amarnath Yatra is one of Hinduism's major annual pilgrimages, drawing hundreds of thousands of devotees each year to a naturally-formed ice stalagmite in a cave shrine 3,880 metres up in the Kashmir Himalayas, revered as a form of Lord Shiva. The route runs through steep, weather-exposed terrain along the Jammu-Srinagar highway and mountain tracks, making it highly vulnerable to landslides and flash floods during the monsoon. Authorities have suspended the Yatra in past years for similar weather reasons and coordinate closely with the Army and disaster-response agencies given the route's difficulty and the pilgrim numbers involved.

stories.title: Trent Rockets cruise past Birmingham Phoenix by 7 wickets to boost their Hundred playoff hopes
stories.what_happened: Birmingham Phoenix batted first and were restricted to 111 for 6 in their 100 balls. Trent Rockets then chased the target down with ease, finishing on 116 for 3 with 17 balls unused, sealing a 7-wicket win in Match 22 of the 2026 competition.
key_points: **Trent Rockets** chased down Birmingham Phoenix's total to win by **7 wickets** in Match 22 of The Hundred.
Birmingham Phoenix were held to **111/6** from their 100 balls after choosing to bat.
Trent Rockets reached **116/3** with **17 balls to spare**, a comfortable chase.
The win boosts Trent Rockets' net run rate as they push for a **top-3 playoff spot**.
The Hundred's playoffs begin in mid-August, making every group game count.

depth.background: **The Hundred** is an English franchise cricket tournament where each innings is exactly 100 balls (rather than the 120 balls of a standard T20), designed to be a faster, more TV-friendly format. Eight city-based men's and women's teams play a short round-robin before the **top three** advance to playoffs. With so few group games, results like this one carry outsized weight for final standings.

stories.title: The Caribbean Premier League kicks off its 2026 season with Jamaica Kingsmen posting 167 in the tournament opener
stories.what_happened: The tournament's 2026 edition opened with a match between Antigua and Barbuda Falcons and Jamaica Kingsmen in Kingstown. Batting first, Jamaica Kingsmen posted 167 for 7 in their 20 overs, setting the target for the Falcons' run chase in the tournament's first game of the season.
key_points: The **2026 Caribbean Premier League (CPL)** began on August 7 in Kingstown, St Vincent.
**Jamaica Kingsmen** batted first against **Antigua and Barbuda Falcons** and posted **167/7** in 20 overs.
The CPL is the Caribbean's flagship T20 tournament, running through **September 20**.
It regularly draws top international players from India, Australia, England and beyond during their franchise 'off-season' windows.
The season-opener sets the tone for six weeks of Caribbean cricket coverage.

depth.background: The **Caribbean Premier League** is a franchise T20 tournament featuring teams representing islands and regions across the West Indies, similar in format to the IPL. It has become a popular stop for international stars during gaps in their home countries' schedules, and strong CPL form is often watched closely ahead of bigger franchise auctions elsewhere.

stories.title: F1's driver market heats up: Alonso wants $46M to stay at Aston Martin, Bearman commits to Ferrari, and Perez's camp explores Williams
stories.what_happened: Reports say Alonso is asking Aston Martin for close to $46 million per season to sign a two-year extension through 2027-2028, a big jump from his current pay that would make him one of the grid's best-paid drivers; rumors of a possible Alpine return are seen as strengthening his negotiating position. Separately, Bearman has reportedly rejected a larger financial offer from Aston Martin, choosing instead to remain in the Ferrari Driver Academy system through 2028. And Pérez's management is reported to be in talks with Williams about a potential seat for 2027 — a move that, if it happens, would directly threaten Sainz's place at the team.
key_points: **Fernando Alonso** is reportedly seeking about **$46 million a season** — up from roughly $35M — to extend at Aston Martin.
That would make him F1's **third-highest-paid driver**, behind only Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen.
**Ollie Bearman** turned down a bigger offer from Aston Martin to stay with **Ferrari** through 2028.
**Sergio Pérez's** management is said to be in talks with **Williams**, a move that could squeeze out Carlos Sainz.
None of these are confirmed deals — F1's driver market rumor mill is intensifying ahead of the 2027 season.

depth.background: Every year, F1's 20 race seats get renegotiated in what fans call the 'driver market' or 'silly season.' **Fernando Alonso**, a two-time world champion now in his 40s, has been Aston Martin's senior driver as the team tries to build toward the front of the grid. **Ollie Bearman** is a young driver contracted to Ferrari's junior academy who has been racing for Haas. **Sergio Pérez**, a former Red Bull driver now on a one-year deal, and **Carlos Sainz**, currently struggling at Williams, are both searching for secure 2027 seats.

stories.title: Christian Horner and Jeremy Clarkson raise £1 million for Chris Hoy's cancer charity in one afternoon
stories.what_happened: Christian Horner organized a clay pigeon shoot and fundraising day at the Marston Estate in Northamptonshire for Sir Chris Hoy's Tour de 4 cancer charity. Jeremy Clarkson hosted the auction portion of the event. Ticket sales, table bookings and the auction raised **£850,000**, and Clarkson personally pushed the total to **£1 million** by directly asking guests who had arrived by helicopter to each contribute **£10,000**. The full amount was raised in a single afternoon.
key_points: Ex-Red Bull boss **Christian Horner** hosted a clay-shooting charity day at his Oxfordshire estate for Olympic legend **Sir Chris Hoy's** cancer charity.
TV host **Jeremy Clarkson** ran the auction and personally pushed the total over the line by asking helicopter-arriving guests for **£10,000 each**.
The event raised **£1 million in a single afternoon**, with **£850,000** coming from tickets, tables and the auction.
Hoy, a **six-time Olympic cycling gold medalist**, is fighting **stage-four prostate cancer** and runs the **Tour de 4** charity.

depth.background: Sir Chris Hoy, one of Britain's most decorated Olympians with six cycling gold medals, revealed in 2024 that he had been diagnosed with terminal prostate cancer. He has since used his platform to raise awareness and funds through his **Tour de 4** charity, framing living with stage-four cancer as something to be met with defiance rather than despair. Christian Horner, who was dismissed as Red Bull's team boss earlier in 2026, has stayed connected to the F1 world through outside ventures like this. Jeremy Clarkson, the former Top Gear host, is a longtime motorsport figure with his own following in the F1 paddock.

stories.title: Hindalco posts its best-ever quarter as aluminium, copper and its US unit Novelis all fire together
stories.what_happened: Hindalco reported its strongest quarter ever: net profit of ₹7,013 crore, up 75% from a year ago, on revenue of ₹84,825 crore. Its **aluminium** upstream business contributed ₹13,403 crore of revenue and its **copper** business ₹17,232 crore. In the US, Novelis delivered a record adjusted EBITDA of ₹4,875 crore, up 37% year-on-year, helped by the successful restart of its **Oswego hot mill** and ongoing cost-cutting.
key_points: **Hindalco Industries'** consolidated net profit jumped **75% year-on-year** to **₹7,013 crore** in Q1 FY27 (April-June).
Consolidated revenue rose to **₹84,825 crore**, up from ₹64,232 crore a year earlier — an all-time high.
EBITDA (core operating profit) surged **73%** to **₹14,989 crore**, split roughly between aluminium and copper.
US subsidiary **Novelis** posted record EBITDA too, helped by its **Oswego, New York hot mill restarting**.
It's the company's **best-ever quarter** on revenue, profit and EBITDA all at once.

depth.background: **Hindalco Industries**, part of the Aditya Birla Group, is India's largest aluminium and copper producer and also owns **Novelis**, a major US-listed recycled-aluminium company that supplies car and beverage-can makers. Metals companies like Hindalco are highly sensitive to global commodity prices — when aluminium and copper prices rise, or when demand from autos and packaging picks up, profits can swing sharply. Novelis had faced production disruptions at some of its US plants in recent quarters, making its recovery an important piece of this result.

stories.title: Sensex sheds 456 points, Nifty slips below 24,600 as financial stocks drag despite a winning week
stories.what_happened: Indian benchmark indices closed lower on Friday, August 7, with the **Sensex down 456 points (0.58%) to 78,499.17** and the **Nifty 50 down 0.27% to 24,570.65**, dragged mainly by a sell-off in financial stocks. **Bank Nifty fell 317 points (0.55%) to 57,746.45**, and the broader financial services sector was the weakest performer, down **1.48%**. Gains in **information technology and auto stocks** partly offset the losses, while elevated crude oil prices and cautious global cues also weighed on sentiment. Despite the Friday dip, both indices closed the week roughly **1% higher**, marking a **second consecutive winning week**. Foreign institutional investors have bought a net **$1.3 billion** of Indian equities so far in August, following **$2.1 billion** in July purchases.
key_points: **Sensex fell 0.58%** to close at **78,499.17**; **Nifty 50 dropped 0.27%** to **24,570.65**.
**Bank Nifty** slid **317 points**, with financial services the **weakest major sector**, down nearly **1.5%**.
Despite Friday's fall, both indices still ended the week **up around 1%**, a **second straight winning week**.
**Foreign investors bought a net $1.3 billion** of Indian stocks so far in August, after **$2.1 billion in July**.

depth.background: Indian markets have been choppy through 2026 as investors weigh **elevated crude oil prices**, global interest-rate uncertainty, and domestic regulatory moves like the RBI's proposed curbs on revolving credit for shadow banks. **FII (foreign institutional investor) flows** — money foreign funds put into or pull out of Indian shares — are a key swing factor for the market's direction, since domestic mutual funds alone can't always offset heavy foreign selling or buying. IT and auto stocks have been relative bright spots recently even as banks and financials wobble.

stories.title: Scotland edge Canada by 9 runs in ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 thriller at Dundee
stories.what_happened: At Forthill in Dundee, Scotland posted 281 for 7 in their 50 overs before bowling out Canada for 272 in 49.2 overs, winning by 9 runs in the 123rd match of the League Two cycle. The narrow margin made it one of the tighter contests in this phase of the competition.
key_points: Scotland posted **281/7**, then bowled Canada out for **272 in 49.2 overs** to win by **9 runs**.
The result was the **123rd match** of the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League Two, a multi-year league for cricket's associate nations.
League Two results feed into **ODI status and future World Cup qualifying pathways** for non-Test-playing nations.
The tight finish keeps both sides in the mix in a league that runs through **2027**.

depth.background: The ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League Two is a long-running multi-year competition among cricket's 'associate' nations — countries like Scotland, Canada, Nepal and Namibia that don't have permanent Test status. Results in this league determine which teams keep official One Day International (ODI) status and which advance toward qualifying for future ICC World Cups, making even routine-looking fixtures like this one carry real stakes for these programmes.

stories.title: Abelardo de la Espriella sworn in as Colombia's first hard-right president in decades
stories.what_happened: De la Espriella was sworn in Friday as Colombia's new head of state after defeating Cepeda, the ruling party's candidate, in June. Unlike every Colombian president for the past two centuries, he chose to be inaugurated in **Cali** rather than the capital, Bogotá, holding the ceremony at a university arena before delivering his first address to the nation from a **military canton** — a symbolic signal of his security-first agenda. About a dozen foreign heads of state attended under heavy security, with **11,000 troops** deployed across the city. He used his first hours in office to promise fiscal discipline and a tougher stance against armed groups operating in Colombia's countryside.
key_points: **Abelardo de la Espriella**, a 48-year-old lawyer nicknamed 'The Tiger,' was inaugurated as Colombia's 36th president on **August 7**.
He beat leftist Senator **Iván Cepeda** by just over **1 percentage point** in a record-turnout June 21 runoff — more than **26 million** votes cast.
He broke **200 years of tradition** by holding the ceremony in **Cali**, not Bogotá, delivering his first address from a military base.
**Donald Trump** endorsed him during the campaign, and roughly **11,000 troops** guarded the inauguration.
He immediately vowed a hard line on armed groups and to '**put a stop to public debt** in the coming hours.'

depth.background: Colombia has been governed since 2022 by **Gustavo Petro**, its first leftist president, who pursued a 'total peace' strategy of negotiating with armed groups and drug-trafficking factions instead of only fighting them. That approach grew unpopular as violence persisted in parts of the country, and it fueled a swing back to the right. De la Espriella built his campaign around **Trump-style hardline rhetoric** — tougher security policy, closer ties to Washington, and skepticism of negotiating with guerrillas. His running mate is **José Manuel Restrepo**.

stories.title: Sunrisers Leeds eliminate Birmingham Phoenix from The Hundred with a 45-run win
stories.what_happened: In the 24th match of the men's competition, Sunrisers Leeds posted **169 for 7** batting first, with Ryan Rickelton's **65** anchoring the innings and earning him Player of the Match. Birmingham Phoenix's chase fell well short, as they were restricted to **124 for 8** in their 100 balls, handing Sunrisers a **45-run win**. The result moves Sunrisers up to second place in the men's standings and mathematically eliminates Phoenix from reaching the playoffs. In the accompanying women's fixture, Sunrisers Leeds Women chased down Birmingham Phoenix Women's total of **107 for 9** with ease, winning by **9 wickets** with 31 balls unused.
key_points: Sunrisers Leeds beat Birmingham Phoenix by **45 runs** in the men's Hundred, scoring **169/7** to Phoenix's **124/8**.
**Ryan Rickelton** was Player of the Match with **65 runs**, continuing his strong form this tournament.
The result **eliminates Birmingham Phoenix** from playoff contention, while Sunrisers move up to **2nd place** in the table.
In the same double-header, Sunrisers Leeds Women also beat Birmingham Phoenix Women by **9 wickets** with 31 balls to spare.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-form domestic cricket competition, using a 100-ball-per-innings format designed to be faster and more broadcast-friendly than standard T20 cricket. Eight men's and women's teams compete each season, with the top teams advancing to playoffs. Birmingham Phoenix and Sunrisers Leeds have both been mid-table teams this season, making a result that eliminates one of them from contention a meaningful moment in the competition's run-in.

stories.title: Red Bull blocks a Williams move to keep Verstappen's next race engineer in-house
stories.what_happened: Red Bull has confirmed that Tom Hart, not an outside hire, will take over as Max Verstappen's race engineer once Lambiase departs. The twist is that Hart had already accepted an offer to move to Williams next season, where he would have engineered Alex Albon's car. When Red Bull realized its own succession plan was about to walk out the door to a direct rival, it asked Williams to release Hart from that agreement — and Williams agreed to unwind the deal. Verstappen said the conversations about Hart taking over began informally around the Miami Grand Prix, and that his main criterion for a race engineer is racing instinct over pure data-nerdery: 'You need to understand racing itself... you need to have the insight to read things properly, the way GP obviously does.' Hart is expected to sit in on the radio for parts of the second half of the 2026 season before officially taking the headset full-time in 2027. Lambiase, meanwhile, remains on track to join McLaren no later than 2028.
key_points: **Tom Hart**, currently Max Verstappen's performance engineer at Red Bull, will become his full **race engineer from 2027**, replacing Gianpiero Lambiase.
Hart had already provisionally agreed to leave for **Williams**, to become Alex Albon's race engineer — Red Bull stepped in and asked Williams to **reverse the transfer**.
Hart, a Red Bull employee since **2012**, will start filling in on the pit-wall radio for **select race weekends in the second half of 2026** ahead of the full 2027 handover.
Verstappen has personally confirmed the choice, saying he and the team had been discussing it since around the **Miami race**.

depth.background: Gianpiero Lambiase has been the voice in Max Verstappen's ear since **2016**, one of the most recognisable driver-engineer pairings in modern F1 and a big part of Verstappen's four world titles. In April 2026, Lambiase announced he is leaving Red Bull to join **McLaren** in 2028 as a senior race-office figure, forcing Red Bull to plan a successor well in advance. Tom Hart was already inside the team as Verstappen's performance engineer — the person who pores over car data between sessions — making him the obvious internal candidate, but he had nearly slipped away to a rival team first.

stories.title: Parliament passes MSME Amendment Bill to fast-track payments to small businesses
stories.what_happened: Parliament completed passage of the **Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026** on Friday, with the Lok Sabha clearing it by voice vote without debate amid Opposition protests over unrelated issues, days after the **Rajya Sabha** passed it earlier in the week. The Bill, moved by MSME Minister **Jitan Ram Manjhi**, makes it mandatory for Central Public Sector Enterprises (government-owned companies) to settle MSME invoices through the **Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS)** — an online platform where small businesses sell unpaid invoices to financiers for instant cash instead of waiting for the buyer to pay. It also tightens dispute timelines: if mediation over a payment dispute fails, the case must go to arbitration within 30 days, and an award must follow within 90 days; if an appeal against that award drags on for more than six months, at least 50% of the awarded amount must be paid to the MSME upfront. Separately, the Bill downgrades many minor registration or reporting lapses from criminal offences to administrative fines ranging from ₹1,000 to ₹1,00,000.
key_points: Parliament passed the **MSME Amendment Bill**, targeting chronic payment delays
Government firms must settle MSME invoices via the **TReDS** platform
Arbitration awards now required within **90 days** of case completion
Minor defaults become fines, not criminal cases, up to **₹1 lakh**
Bill covers India's **6.53 crore** registered MSME units

depth.background: India has about **6.53 crore** registered micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) — a count that has grown roughly 15-fold over the past decade as formal **Udyam** registration expanded — and the sector contributes close to **30% of India's GDP**. A chronic problem for these businesses is late payment: large corporate and government buyers often take months to pay small suppliers, starving them of cash. Existing law already sets payment deadlines, but slow, expensive dispute resolution has blunted enforcement.

stories.title: Sunrisers Leeds Women thrash Birmingham Phoenix by 9 wickets to boost Hundred knockout hopes
stories.what_happened: Sunrisers Leeds Women beat Birmingham Phoenix Women by 9 wickets in Match 24 of the Hundred Women's Competition at Edgbaston, Birmingham on August 7. Birmingham Phoenix were held to 107/9 from their 100 balls, and Sunrisers Leeds chased the target down in just 13.4 overs, finishing on 111/1. Phoebe Litchfield anchored the chase with an unbeaten 71 off 33 balls and was named Player of the Match. The comfortable win strengthens Sunrisers Leeds' position in the race for the two automatic and eliminator knockout spots.
key_points: Sunrisers Leeds Women chased down **107/9** in just **13.4 overs**, finishing **111/1** to win by **9 wickets** at Edgbaston.
**Phoebe Litchfield** starred with an unbeaten **71 off 33 balls**, earning Player of the Match.
The win keeps Sunrisers firmly in the **knockout qualification race**, with the top team going straight to the Lord's final on **August 16**.
Birmingham Phoenix's playoff hopes take a further hit after already-tight qualification scenarios in the Women's Hundred.

depth.background: The Hundred is England's franchise cricket competition, running men's and women's tournaments in parallel each August with eight teams apiece. In the women's competition, the top-placed team after the group stage qualifies directly for the final at Lord's, while second and third play an eliminator for the other final spot — meaning results in these closing group games carry heavy playoff weight. Sunrisers Leeds and Birmingham Phoenix entered this match both needing points to keep their qualification hopes alive.

stories.title: David Coulthard calls Williams' 2026 season a 'write-off' after a miserable first half
stories.what_happened: Ex-F1 driver and pundit David Coulthard declared Williams' 2026 campaign 'effectively a write-off' after the team's disastrous opening 11 races. Williams became the only team to miss the pre-season shakedown test in Barcelona, after delays left it unable to get its car to the track on time; when it finally arrived, the car was significantly overweight and lacking performance. The team has managed only 11 points across the first half of the season, a sharp fall from its 2025 form.
key_points: Former F1 driver **David Coulthard says Williams' season is already a write-off** after 11 rounds.
Williams has scored just **11 points**, leaving it near the bottom of the constructors' table.
The team **missed pre-season testing entirely**, arriving with a car that was overweight and off the pace.
It's a stunning reversal from last year's **surprise 5th-place constructors' finish**.

depth.background: Williams enjoyed a resurgence in 2025, finishing a surprise fifth in the constructors' championship after years near the back of the F1 grid. Heading into 2026's all-new power-unit and chassis regulations — a rules reset every team had to navigate from scratch — many expected the team to build on that momentum. Instead, Williams has struggled badly, and star driver Carlos Sainz's future at the team has also come under question this season.

stories.title: Supreme Court tells states to reserve government jobs for cadets disabled during military training
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court directed states and Union Territories to consider extending the **reservation quota reserved for ex-servicemen** to cadets who are discharged from training due to disabling injuries. It held that cadets with a benchmark disability of 40% or more already qualify for reservation under the 2016 disabilities law, and separately instructed the Union government to design a dedicated welfare scheme for cadets whose disability falls below that threshold. The Ministry of Defence has already extended lifetime ECHS medical coverage to invalided cadets. The court will review compliance from states at the next hearing on September 8.
key_points: The Supreme Court urged **all states and Union Territories** to extend the ex-servicemen job quota to cadets discharged over training injuries.
Cadets with a **'benchmark disability' of 40% or more** are separately entitled to reservation under the **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016**.
The Centre must design a **welfare scheme** for cadets hurt below that 40% threshold, who currently fall outside the disabilities law's protection.
The **Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme** will now cover invalided cadets' medical expenses **for life**.
The matter returns to court on **September 8** for a compliance update.

depth.background: Military cadets who suffer serious injuries during training — before they've formally joined the armed forces — have long occupied a legal grey zone in India: too injured to serve, but not technically 'ex-servicemen,' so they've historically missed out on the job reservations and pension benefits available to those discharged after active duty. The Supreme Court took up a batch of petitions from cadets 'out-boarded' (discharged) after training injuries who argued this gap left them without support just as their careers and health took a permanent hit.

stories.title: Delhi's BJP government tables CAG audit reports on the previous AAP administration's finances
stories.what_happened: Delhi's Legislative Assembly began its **Monsoon Session** today, running through August 11. Chief Minister and Finance Minister Rekha Gupta is set to table two CAG reports: **Report No. 1 of 2026**, covering the financial year ended March 31, 2023 — a period under the previous AAP government — and **Report No. 2 of 2026**, covering overall state finances for 2024-25. The session's business advisory committee has also listed three new bills, covering time-bound delivery of public services, the Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board, and regulation of bed-and-breakfast establishments.
key_points: Delhi's Monsoon Assembly session runs **August 7 to 11**.
CM Rekha Gupta will table **two CAG reports** — one covering the year ended **March 2023**.
A second report covers **state finances for 2024-25**.
Three new bills on public services, urban shelter, and bed-and-breakfast rules are also listed.
The 2023-period report covers spending under the **previous AAP government**.

depth.background: The **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** is India's independent government auditor, responsible for scrutinizing how public money is spent by the central and state governments. Delhi's government changed hands in 2025, when the BJP under **Rekha Gupta** took over from the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), which had run Delhi for over a decade. CAG reports on the AAP years — especially on contested issues like the now-scrapped excise (liquor) policy — have previously become major political flashpoints, since a critical CAG report can be used to allege financial mismanagement by the outgoing government.

stories.title: State Bank of India's profit jumps 10% to ₹21,121 crore, its best-ever quarter
stories.what_happened: State Bank of India reported that its net profit for the April-June 2026 quarter rose **10.23% year-on-year to ₹21,121 crore**, up from ₹19,160 crore a year earlier and up 7.3% from the March 2026 quarter. Net interest income (NII) — the difference between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits — grew **14.88%** to ₹46,992 crore from ₹40,907 crore a year ago. Asset quality improved, with the gross non-performing asset (bad loan) ratio falling to **1.47%** from 1.83%, and net NPA improving to 0.38% from 0.47%. Gross advances — the total loans on SBI's books — grew **18.63%** to ₹50.47 lakh crore as of June 2026. SBI's stock rose 3.5% in reaction to the results.
key_points: SBI's Q1 FY27 net profit rose **10.23% year-on-year** to **₹21,121 crore**, up from ₹19,160 crore a year earlier.
Net interest income — the bank's core lending profit — jumped **14.88%** to **₹46,992 crore**.
Asset quality improved: the gross bad-loan ratio fell to **1.47%** from 1.83% a year ago.
Gross advances (total loans) grew **18.63%** year-on-year to **₹50.47 lakh crore**.
SBI shares gained **3.5%** on the results.

depth.background: State Bank of India is India's largest bank by assets and a **public-sector undertaking (PSU)** — majority owned by the government — making its health a bellwether for the broader Indian banking system and the economy's ability to fund growth. Q1 results (April-June) are the first quarterly report card of the new financial year (FY27) and are watched closely for signs of whether Indian banks are still lending freely or pulling back amid global uncertainty. SBI has posted a mostly upward profit trend in recent years as bad-loan levels across Indian banking have fallen sharply from the stressed period of the mid-2010s.

stories.title: Teenage gunman kills 7, wounds ~15 at a Bangkok-area school after murdering his grandparents
stories.what_happened: Police say the teenage suspect first shot and killed his **grandparents** at their home in Bang Bua Thong before travelling to Debsirin School in Bang Kruai district, Nonthaburi province, and opening fire on students and staff. He killed **seven people** in total and injured roughly **15 others** — some reports put the injury count over 30 when including people hurt in the panic and evacuation — before he was killed himself (officials say he took his own life). Investigators are still trying to establish exactly how the 14-year-old gained access to his grandfather's handgun and whether there were any warning signs beforehand. The attack triggered a mass emergency response, with the school placed on lockdown and injured students taken to nearby hospitals.
key_points: A **14-year-old student** opened fire at Debsirin School in Bang Kruai, Nonthaburi (just outside Bangkok), around **10am on Friday, August 7**.
He killed **7 people** — reportedly including teachers and students — and wounded around **15 more** before the rampage ended.
Before going to school, he had already shot and killed his **own grandparents** at their home, where he lived and where the handgun — belonging to his grandfather — was kept.
It is Thailand's **worst mass killing since the 2022 Nong Bua Lamphu massacre**, which killed 38 people, mostly children.

depth.background: Thailand has comparatively strict gun-licensing laws on paper, but enforcement is uneven and firearms — especially older, family-owned handguns like the one used here — circulate widely outside formal channels. The country has still suffered a string of mass-casualty shootings this decade, including the 2022 Nong Bua Lamphu attack, which prompted promises of tighter gun control that were only partly followed through on. Nonthaburi is a dense suburb bordering the capital, Bangkok, and Debsirin School is a well-known, long-established institution, which is part of why this attack has shocked the country so deeply.

stories.title: Kuldeep Yadav and Ravindra Jadeja spin out Sri Lanka Board XI for 187 on Day 1 of India's warm-up
stories.what_happened: On the opening day of the warm-up match, India's spinners dominated, with Kuldeep Yadav taking four wickets and Ravindra Jadeja three to dismiss the Sri Lanka Board President's XI for 187. In India's reply, stand-in captain KL Rahul anchored the innings with a well-made 54 as India closed the day on 135 for 3, trailing by 52 runs. Gill did not take the field but is expected to be assessed ahead of the rest of the match.
key_points: India's spinners **Kuldeep Yadav (4 wickets) and Ravindra Jadeja (3 wickets)** bowled out a Sri Lanka Board President's XI for **187**.
**KL Rahul**, standing in as captain for the injured Shubman Gill, top-scored with **54** as India reached 135/3 in reply.
The three-day match at Colombo's **Nondescripts Cricket Club** is India's only warm-up before the **first Test in Galle on August 15**.
Gill sat out the opening day as a **precaution** after an impact injury to his right ring finger in training.

depth.background: India are touring Sri Lanka for a Test series beginning August 15 in Galle, and this three-day fixture against a Sri Lanka Board President's XI is their only warm-up match before it. Shubman Gill, India's Test captain, picked up a finger injury during a practice session just before the match and was withheld from the opening day as a precaution, handing the reins to vice-captain KL Rahul. India's spin attack, built around Ravindra Jadeja and the returning Kuldeep Yadav, is central to the team's plans on traditionally spin-friendly Sri Lankan pitches.

stories.title: Shubman Gill's India begin their Sri Lanka tour with a three-day warm-up match in Colombo
stories.what_happened: India's touring Test squad, led by **Shubman Gill**, began a **three-day warm-up match** against a **Sri Lanka Cricket XI** at the Nondescripts Cricket Club (NCC) ground in Colombo on **August 7**, after the fixture was trimmed from its originally planned four days. The squad had arrived in Colombo on **August 4** and used the days since for practice sessions to acclimatize to local conditions. This tour game is the final preparation step before India's **two-match Test series** against Sri Lanka, with the first Test scheduled for **August 15–19 in Galle** and the second for **August 23–27 in Colombo** at the Sinhalese Sports Club (SSC).
key_points: India's Test squad, led by **Shubman Gill**, opened a **three-day warm-up match** against a Sri Lanka Cricket XI at the **Nondescripts Cricket Club (NCC)** in Colombo on August 7.
The warm-up was **shortened from four days to three** ahead of the main Test series.
It sets up India's **two-match Test series** against Sri Lanka: the first Test starts **August 15 in Galle**, the second **August 23 in Colombo** (SSC).
The squad **arrived in Colombo on August 4** and has been going through practice sessions since.
This is India's first away Test assignment since the squad transition under **Gill's captaincy** continues to take shape.

depth.background: Warm-up (or 'tour') matches are practice fixtures a touring cricket team plays against a local invitational side before a Test series begins — they let batters adjust to unfamiliar pitch and weather conditions and give bowlers match rhythm without the pressure of a series-deciding game. India's tour of Sri Lanka comes as the team continues to settle into its post-transition era under **Shubman Gill's** Test captaincy, and Sri Lankan conditions — typically low, slow, and spin-friendly — pose a different challenge than what Indian batters see at home.

stories.title: UN warns of 'mass atrocities' as drone siege and cholera engulf Sudan's El Obeid
stories.what_happened: Aid groups including **Doctors Without Borders (MSF)** and UN officials say the RSF has spent recent months tightening a siege around El Obeid, using swarms of drones to strike the infrastructure civilians depend on to survive rather than just military targets. Water pumping stations, wells and the city's main power station have all been hit, and residents describe drone attacks happening even on routine daytime errands. With safe routes to water cut, women and girls say they increasingly wait until dark to fetch it, when attacks are thought less likely — but aid workers report a corresponding rise in sexual violence carried out under cover of that same darkness. Meanwhile a **cholera** outbreak that began in neighboring West Kordofan state in May, and has already killed more than 120 people there, has now spread into North Kordofan, with cases confirmed in and around El Obeid where crippled water and health systems make treatment far harder. UN humanitarian officials briefed the Security Council this week that roughly **500,000 residents plus close to 100,000 people already displaced by earlier fighting** are effectively encircled, and formally warned of a "serious risk of mass atrocities" if the city falls the way El Fasher did.
key_points: The paramilitary **Rapid Support Forces (RSF)** are besieging El Obeid, a city of roughly **500,000 people**, with residents reporting as many as **40 drones** in the sky at once.
UN experts warn the city could see a repeat of **El Fasher**, the Darfur city where the RSF killed an estimated **6,000 civilians** after it fell in 2025.
Drone strikes have hit **water points, a market, fuel stations, schools and the main power station**, crippling the city's ability to function.
A cholera outbreak that has already killed over **120 people** in neighboring West Kordofan has now crossed into North Kordofan, where El Obeid sits.
Nearly **100,000 people** already displaced by earlier fighting are trapped inside the city alongside residents, with water prices roughly **doubling**.

depth.background: Sudan has been at war since **April 2023**, when the regular army (SAF) and the paramilitary **RSF** — a force descended from the Janjaweed militias notorious from the 2000s Darfur genocide — turned on each other after jointly ruling the country following a coup. The conflict has since split Sudan roughly in two, with the RSF dominant across Darfur and pushing into central Sudan. In late 2025 the RSF seized the Darfur city of **El Fasher** after a long siege, and international investigators say its fighters then carried out mass killings, rape and ethnic-targeted violence against civilians who could not flee. El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, sits on the main road between Darfur and the capital Khartoum, making it the next major prize — and, aid groups fear, the next El Fasher.

stories.title: FIA's next big target for F1 cars: another 80kg off the scales
stories.what_happened: Speaking about how the 2026 cars have turned out, Tombazis said: 'The cars are a bit lighter and a bit smaller, which the drivers have appreciated. Now, is that where I would like us to be? No. I would like us to be another 80 kilos lighter, and maybe still a bit shorter and a bit smaller.' That would be well over double the 32kg the sport just fought to remove this year. He tied the ambition to the next full regulation cycle, which is currently pencilled in for 2031 (or 2030 if teams agree to move faster), and said the FIA also wants **simpler, cheaper power units** in that next generation of rules, plus tighter policing so clever team loopholes cannot undermine the intent of the regulations the way they have in the past.
key_points: FIA single-seater director **Nikolas Tombazis** says he wants F1 cars to shed **another 80kg** under the sport's next major rules overhaul.
The 2026 cars already dropped **32kg** to a new minimum weight of **768kg** — the first time in decades F1 cars got lighter instead of heavier.
The bigger 80kg cut is targeted for the next full regulation reset, due in **2031**, or **2030** if enough teams back an earlier switch.
Tombazis also wants **simpler power units** and possibly a **shorter, smaller** car alongside the extra weight loss.

depth.background: F1 cars ballooned in size and weight for roughly three decades as hybrid power units, crash-safety structures, and wider tyres piled on mass, hurting overtaking and increasing tyre wear and the physical toll on drivers. For 2026, the FIA (F1's regulator) forced through the sport's first-ever weight reduction, alongside smaller car dimensions, specifically to make racing more agile. That 2026 reset was seen as a hard-fought first step, not a finish line.

stories.title: Ajinkya Rahane signs with Steve Waugh's Amsterdam Flames for cricket's new European T20 league, days after retiring from India duty
stories.what_happened: Amsterdam Flames announced on Friday, August 7, that they have signed Ajinkya Rahane as their marquee player for the first-ever season of the European T20 Premier League, a new six-team franchise competition featuring city-based sides from Glasgow, Amsterdam, Edinburgh, Dublin, Belfast and Rotterdam, running August 26 to September 20. The signing comes barely a week after Rahane announced his retirement from international cricket and all formats on July 30, ending a career of 85 Tests, 90 ODIs and 20 T20Is for India. Steve Waugh, the Amsterdam Flames co-founder and Chief Cricket Officer and a former Australia Test captain, reportedly called Rahane just five minutes after his retirement announcement to recruit him personally, saying Rahane "represents everything you want in a professional cricketer — skill, resilience, humility and leadership." Rahane, for his part, spoke of admiring Waugh and wanting to share his experience in a new cricket market.
key_points: Former India Test vice-captain **Ajinkya Rahane** has been unveiled as **Amsterdam Flames'** marquee signing for the inaugural **European T20 Premier League (ETPL)**.
The six-team ETPL runs **August 26 to September 20, 2026**, featuring city sides from Amsterdam, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Dublin, Belfast and Rotterdam.
The move comes barely a week after Rahane **retired from all international cricket on July 30**, having played 85 Tests, 90 ODIs and 20 T20Is for India.
Amsterdam Flames co-founder **Steve Waugh**, the former Australia captain, reportedly called Rahane just **five minutes after his retirement announcement** to recruit him.
Waugh called Rahane's game **"skill, resilience, humility and leadership"** — the qualities he wants anchoring the new franchise.

depth.background: A "marquee player" in franchise T20 leagues is a headline signing used to anchor a new team's brand identity and draw fans and sponsors — typically a recognisable international name rather than necessarily the league's best current player. The ETPL is a brand-new competition aiming to grow professional T20 cricket in non-traditional European markets, following the same playbook that expanded the sport into the US and Gulf through leagues like Major League Cricket. Rahane, who turns 38 in 2026, was India's long-serving Test vice-captain and a member of the 2013 Champions Trophy-winning squad, best known for gritty overseas Test centuries including a standout 2020-21 series in Australia.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty open lower as crude oil climbs on fresh Middle East tensions
stories.what_happened: India's benchmark indices opened lower on Friday, with the **Sensex falling 438.68 points (0.55%) to 78,516.08** and the **Nifty shedding 97.1 points to 24,538.90**. The declines came as crude oil prices rose on renewed Middle East tensions — including the deadly Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces and the unresolved Strait of Hormuz standoff — and as Asian markets broadly fell after a weak US session overnight. Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped over 370 points (0.57%) in sympathy. **Foreign institutional investors were net sellers for a second consecutive session**, while domestic institutional investors continued buying, partly offsetting the selling pressure. Broader mid-cap and small-cap indices were comparatively resilient, trading with only minor gains.
key_points: Sensex tumbled **438.68 points (0.55%)** to open at **78,516.08**; Nifty fell **97.1 points** to **24,538.90**.
The drop tracks **rising crude oil prices** as Middle East tensions escalate — India imports over 80% of its oil.
**FIIs sold for a second straight day** while domestic institutional investors kept buying, cushioning the fall.
Asian markets fell in sympathy, with Japan's **Nikkei down over 370 points**.

depth.background: India is one of the world's largest oil importers, so its stock market and currency are highly sensitive to swings in crude prices — a jump in oil directly raises India's import bill, widens its **current-account deficit**, and squeezes companies' fuel costs. Markets had already been jittery this week over the Strait of Hormuz standoff and the deadly escalation in Yemen, both threatening Middle East oil supply routes. **Foreign institutional investors (FIIs)** have been net sellers of Indian equities recently, while **domestic institutional investors (DIIs)** — mutual funds, insurers, pension funds — have stepped in as buyers, a pattern that has repeatedly cushioned Indian markets this year.

stories.title: F1 boss says more Sprint races are coming in 2027, whether fans like it or not
stories.what_happened: Speaking as F1 enters its summer break, Domenicali said the sport now expects to run **more Sprint races in 2027** than the current six, though he did not confirm an exact number. He said the format has proven itself commercially, boosting both **Friday attendance** and overall race-weekend crowds at host venues, and that F1 has been fielding requests from fans and race promoters who want meaningful on-track action across all three days of a weekend, not just practice. At the same time, he pushed back on going all-in, arguing that Sprints partly work *because* they are rare: "the scarcity is a value," he said, warning that running them everywhere would erode that appeal. That puts him at odds with Alpine team principal **Flavio Briatore**, who told reporters he would run a Sprint at every single round: "For me, 24 races, 24 sprint races." Some reports suggest F1 is weighing as many as nine or ten Sprint weekends for 2027 — nearly half the calendar — though nothing is officially locked in yet.
key_points: F1 CEO **Stefano Domenicali** confirms Sprint races will expand in **2027**
There are currently **six** Sprint weekends out of 24 races in 2026
Domenicali says Sprints drive **higher Friday attendance** at race venues
Alpine boss **Flavio Briatore** wants Sprints at **all 24** race weekends
Full details on the new Sprint count expected to be released **soon**

depth.background: A **Sprint** is a shortened, roughly 100-kilometre race — about a third the length of a normal Grand Prix — held on the Saturday of certain race weekends, with its own separate, shorter qualifying session (called Sprint Qualifying) on the Friday. It was introduced in 2021 to give fans more on-track action across a race weekend instead of just practice sessions on Fridays, and in 2026 there are six Sprint weekends: China, Miami, Canada, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and Singapore. F1's commercial rights holder, **Liberty Media**, and team bosses have debated for years how far to expand the format without diluting the main Grand Prix's importance.

stories.title: Red Bull rated 5 out of 10 at midseason — still winless with its first in-house engine
stories.what_happened: Respected F1 technical analyst Rob Smedley handed Red Bull a mid-season rating of 5 out of 10, saying the team has been dogged by a rotating cast of 'basic problems' — balance issues, inconsistent race pace, and power-unit faults — with something different going wrong nearly every weekend. Despite this, Verstappen has still managed podium finishes when the car has held together, but neither he nor teammate Isack Hadjar has won a race in the first 11 rounds of 2026.
key_points: Ex-F1 technical chief **Rob Smedley gave Red Bull a 5/10** midseason rating.
He says the team has hit a **'different basic problem' almost every race weekend** in 2026.
2026 is Red Bull's **first year building its own power unit**, in partnership with Ford — reliability has fallen short of expectations.
**Max Verstappen has scored podiums but zero wins** so far this season.

depth.background: Red Bull dominated F1 for years while buying its engines from outside suppliers. For 2026's new power-unit rules, the team took the ambitious step of designing and building its own engine in-house for the first time, in partnership with Ford — a huge technical undertaking that many rivals also attempted under the reset regulations. Early results suggested the switch would be bumpy, and Max Verstappen has publicly voiced frustration over reliability issues, including a rear-wing failure that caused multiple spins and crashes.

stories.title: CBI says NEET-UG 2026's medical entrance exam was leaked by the government's own paper-setting experts
stories.what_happened: The CBI has filed a chargesheet naming **13 people** in what it describes as a coordinated, multi-state conspiracy to leak the NEET-UG 2026 question paper. Three of the accused — Botany expert **Manisha Gurunath Mandhare**, Chemistry expert **Prahlad Vithalrao Kulkarni**, and Physics expert **Manisha Sanjay Havaldar** — were NTA-appointed subject experts responsible for setting and translating the exam. CBI alleges they were **cultivated months before the exam** in exchange for money, and that they memorized simpler questions to write down later, while one of them used rough sheets given during translation work to secretly list all **135 questions** as small chits. Those leaked questions were then allegedly circulated through a network of **coaching centre operators, brokers, and intermediaries** to candidates willing to pay.
key_points: CBI has charged **13 people** in a multi-state NEET-UG 2026 paper leak racket.
Three of them are **NTA-appointed subject experts** — the officials trusted to set the actual exam.
CBI says the leak was **planned months in advance**, not a last-minute breach.
Experts allegedly **memorized questions** and smuggled details out on chits and rough sheets.
Leaked questions were sold through a network of **coaching operators and brokers**.

depth.background: NEET-UG is India's single national entrance exam for admission to medical colleges — one of the most high-stakes, competitive tests in the country, taken by well over a million students a year. It's run by the **National Testing Agency (NTA)**, a government body created specifically to run large-scale entrance exams securely. NEET has been hit by leak scandals before, including a major 2024 controversy that triggered nationwide protests and court cases. This is a fresh leak tied to the **2026 exam cycle**, and it's more damaging than past cases because it implicates the NTA's own subject-matter experts — the very people meant to guard exam integrity — rather than outside hackers or printers.

stories.title: US employers unexpectedly cut jobs in July, unemployment rate falls to 4.1%
stories.what_happened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday that US nonfarm payrolls **fell by 23,000** in July 2026, a sharp miss against expectations of roughly an 80,000 gain. The unemployment rate ticked down to **4.1%**, but only because labor-force participation slid as fewer Americans actively looked for work. The bureau also cut its estimates for May and June by a combined **103,000 jobs**, meaning the economy created far fewer jobs this spring than first reported. Losses were concentrated in local government education and retail trade, while healthcare employment kept climbing and wage growth slowed. Markets read the report as confirmation that the labor market is weaker than the government's own real-time data had been showing.
key_points: Nonfarm payrolls fell by **23,000** in July, defying expectations of a modest gain.
The unemployment rate still dropped to **4.1%**, mainly because more people left the labor force entirely.
May and June payroll figures were revised down by a combined **103,000** jobs.
Job losses were concentrated in **local government education** and retail trade, while healthcare kept adding jobs.
The report lands weeks before the Fed's **September meeting**, raising the odds of a rate cut.

depth.background: The US jobs report, officially the Employment Situation, is released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on the first Friday of most months and is the single most-watched economic data point in the world — it tells investors, the Federal Reserve, and the White House whether the world's largest economy is still creating work faster than it's losing it. Coming into today, other data had hinted at a cooling labor market, but forecasters still expected a modest bounce-back after a soft spring. Instead the headline number came in negative, and prior months were revised sharply lower, meaning the slowdown was worse than anyone realized in real time. **A falling unemployment rate even as jobs disappear** is not automatically good news — it often happens when discouraged workers give up looking for work and simply stop being counted.

stories.title: Delhi's heaviest August rain in years floods streets, collapses houses
stories.what_happened: Heavy rain battered Delhi through Thursday night and into Friday morning, prompting the IMD to issue a **red alert** — its most severe rainfall warning — for the city. The 24 hours ending 8:30am Friday saw the **heaviest August rainfall Delhi has recorded so far this year**, with weather stations across the city logging between roughly 17mm and 60mm of rain. Streets flooded, traffic was disrupted across the National Capital Region, and the Delhi Fire Service recorded at least 9 house collapses and 16 fallen trees. In flood-prone neighbourhoods such as Valmiki Basti, residents were seen wading through waist-deep water, with some using plastic sheets as makeshift rafts to move children through flooded lanes.
key_points: The India Meteorological Department (**IMD**) issued a **red alert** for Delhi as overnight rain kept pouring through Friday.
The capital logged its **rainiest day of August so far this year**, with **Lodhi Road recording 60.4mm** and Safdarjung 59.2mm in the 24 hours to 8:30am.
At least **9 houses collapsed** and **16 trees fell** across the city since Thursday night, per the Delhi Fire Service.
Residents in low-lying areas like Valmiki Basti waded through **waist-deep water**, with some carrying schoolchildren across flooded lanes on plastic sheets.

depth.background: Delhi's monsoon drainage system is old and frequently overwhelmed even by moderate rain, because much of the city's stormwater infrastructure predates its explosive population growth. This is part of a wider pattern this monsoon season: other parts of India — including Kerala and Odisha — have also been hit by red-alert-level rain and flooding in the past week, as an active monsoon trough and a low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal push heavy rain across much of the country. Waterlogging, traffic chaos, and structural damage from heavy rain are a near-annual occurrence in Delhi, but this spell has been unusually intense for August.

stories.title: US formally requests Quiboloy's extradition from the Philippines on sex-trafficking charges
stories.what_happened: The US government has now formally transmitted its extradition request for Quiboloy to the Philippine Department of Justice, more than a year after his arrest. Philippine Ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez said Washington wants him extradited **'as soon as possible.'** The request, tied to the 2021 California indictment, covers charges of **sex trafficking of minors, fraud and smuggling over $6 million in cash out of the US.** However, Quiboloy is simultaneously facing Philippine charges of qualified human trafficking and child sexual abuse, and President Marcos has indicated he believes those domestic cases should be resolved before any extradition is finalized. The Philippine DOJ is now reviewing the US request alongside its own prosecution.
key_points: The **US State Department formally requested extradition** of Filipino televangelist Apollo Quiboloy, transmitting the request through the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs.
He faces a **2021 US federal indictment** in California for sex trafficking of minors, fraud, and bulk cash smuggling.
Philippine President **Marcos wants Quiboloy's local criminal cases resolved first**, which could delay any handover for years.
Quiboloy is already in **Philippine government custody** facing separate qualified human-trafficking and child-abuse charges.

depth.background: Apollo Quiboloy is the founder of the **Kingdom of Jesus Christ**, a Philippine-based megachurch with millions of followers and considerable political influence — he was a vocal supporter of former president Rodrigo Duterte. US prosecutors indicted him in 2021, accusing him of running a decades-long scheme in which young female followers ('pastorals') were coerced into sex acts and forced labor under threat of eternal damnation. He evaded arrest for years before Philippine police finally detained him in **September 2024** after a weeks-long standoff at his compound.

stories.title: WA and Perth Scorchers quick Matt Kelly retires from elite cricket at 31 after recurring injuries
stories.what_happened: Matt Kelly has announced his retirement from elite cricket, ending a decade-long career with Western Australia and the Perth Scorchers after being hampered by recent recurring injuries. Across 54 Sheffield Shield matches he took 172 wickets at an average of 25.80, ranking him inside WA's all-time top 20 wicket-takers in the competition. He played 29 List A matches for WA and 39 Big Bash League games for the Scorchers since debuting in BBL|07, taking 55 wickets at an average of 20.54 in the franchise format. Kelly was a key part of WA's hat-trick of Sheffield Shield titles from 2021-22 through 2023-24, highlighted by a six-wicket haul in the 2022-23 final win over Victoria as part of a 35-wicket season at an average of 15.77. In his retirement statement, Kelly thanked his teammates and said he had "loved every minute" of his career.
key_points: Matt Kelly, 31, has retired from **first-class, List A and T20 cricket** after a decade-long career, citing recurring injuries.
He took **172 wickets at 25.80** across 54 Sheffield Shield matches, placing him inside WA's **all-time top 20 wicket-takers**.
Kelly was part of Western Australia's **hat-trick of Sheffield Shield titles from 2021-22 to 2023-24**.
He took **six wickets in the 2022-23 final** win over Victoria, part of a 35-wicket season at 15.77.
For the Perth Scorchers in the Big Bash League he claimed **55 wickets at 20.54** across 39 games since debuting in BBL|07.

depth.background: The Sheffield Shield is Australia's premier first-class (multi-day) domestic competition contested between the six state teams; List A is domestic one-day cricket, and the Big Bash League (BBL) is Australia's franchise Twenty20 league, of which the Perth Scorchers is one of eight teams. In Australian cricket slang, a "quick" means a fast bowler. Finishing inside a state's all-time top 20 wicket-takers is a marker of a genuinely productive career, not just a long one.

stories.title: Kerala flood death toll climbs to 20 as IMD issues fresh red alert for seven districts
stories.what_happened: Kerala remains in the grip of severe monsoon flooding that began roughly a week ago, with the confirmed death toll rising to 20 and 7 people still missing as of Friday, August 7. Pathanamthitta and Kottayam districts have been hit hardest — in Thiruvarppu panchayat alone, 7,924 of 8,064 houses (98%) were inundated after the Meenachil river burst its banks, and in Ranni, floodwaters that had briefly receded began rising again as the Pamba river swelled further. The state has deployed 14 rescue boats between Kollam and Pathanamthitta and kept two helicopters on standby at Sulur, alongside NDRF teams and Army units from Kannur and Wayanad. More than 11,000 people are now in relief camps statewide. The India Meteorological Department's Friday morning nowcast bulletin issued a red alert — the highest warning level, meaning over 15mm of rain per hour with gusts up to 50 kmph — for seven districts: Alappuzha, Kottayam, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Kannur and Kasaragod, with an orange alert for five more including Pathanamthitta. Five dams are also on red alert, and schools remain shut across multiple districts even as floodwaters have begun receding in parts of Kottayam, Pathanamthitta and Alappuzha.
key_points: The death toll from Kerala's monsoon flooding has risen to **20**, with **7 people still missing**.
In Thiruvarppu panchayat (Kottayam), **98% of houses (7,924 of 8,064)** were inundated after the Meenachil river overflowed.
IMD's Friday morning bulletin issued a **red alert for seven districts** — Alappuzha, Kottayam, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Kannur and Kasaragod.
More than **11,000 people** are in relief camps statewide, with **14 rescue boats and 2 standby helicopters** deployed.
**5 dams** are on red alert as authorities warn floodwaters could still worsen despite some easing in Kottayam and Alappuzha.

depth.background: Kerala's monsoon season (June–September) regularly brings destructive flooding because of its hilly, river-dense terrain, and the catastrophic 2018 floods — nearly 500 dead — remain the benchmark comparison; some local reports say specific pockets of this year's flooding, like Thiruvarppu, have exceeded 2018 levels. The current flooding began around August 2-3, driven by swollen rivers including the Meenachil and Pamba, and landslide risk compounds the danger in the Western Ghats districts.

stories.title: Russia's overnight strikes destroy equipment at seven Ukrainian gas facilities
stories.what_happened: Ukrainian officials said overnight strikes destroyed equipment essential to Naftogaz's oil-and-gas extraction operations across **seven separate production facilities** in the country's east, describing it as one of the most damaging attacks on the sector in recent months. No casualties were reported at the gas sites, but multiple facilities had to suspend production. Russian forces also struck four Ukrnafta fuel stations elsewhere. In Washington, the US Senate opened debate on a Russia sanctions bill that has been stuck for over a year, with a possible vote later on August 7.
key_points: Russian drones and missiles hit **seven Naftogaz gas-production sites** in eastern Ukraine overnight, destroying critical extraction equipment.
Several sites were **forced offline**, and separate strikes hit **four fuel stations** in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions in the past 24 hours.
It's part of **287 attacks on Ukraine's gas industry so far in 2026** — already more than the total recorded in all of 2025.
Separately, the **US Senate began floor debate on a long-stalled Russia sanctions bill**, with a vote possible the same day.

depth.background: Naftogaz is Ukraine's state-owned oil and gas company and the backbone of the country's domestic energy supply, heating most Ukrainian homes through the winter. Since Russia's full-scale invasion, Moscow has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy grid and gas-production infrastructure as the cold months approach, aiming to break civilian morale and strain the economy. A **Russia sanctions bill has sat stalled in the US Congress since April 2025**, held up in part by President Trump's shifting approach to the war.

stories.title: Iran and Oman's Hormuz shipping deal enters final drafting — reportedly on Iran's terms
stories.what_happened: Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said on August 7 that a joint statement between Tehran and Muscat on reopening the Strait of Hormuz is under review and in its **final drafting stage**. Reporting from Fortune and CNN describes the emerging deal as recognizing **Iran's control** over the route, a notable shift from the US's earlier insistence on 'no impediments and no fees' for shipping. The deal would set up inbound and outbound lanes through both Iran's and Oman's territorial waters, plus a joint coordination center to track vessel traffic. Iran maintains the arrangement would let it collect service fees and reportedly still wants to restrict passage for US- and Israeli-linked ships — the sticking point that stalled talks for weeks. Baghaei said negotiations remain 'forward-moving' but cautioned a deal would only be struck 'if certain third parties do not obstruct this process,' a reference to Washington.
key_points: A joint Iran-Oman statement on reopening the **Strait of Hormuz** is now in its **final drafting stage**, Iran's foreign ministry says.
Reporting says the emerging deal **effectively accepts Iran's terms** for the shipping route, a shift from Washington's earlier refusal to accept 'impediments.'
The **Strait of Hormuz** carries roughly a **fifth of the world's oil and gas** shipments — the deal sets up a joint coordination center to manage traffic.
President Trump has previously balked at any deal giving Iran more control; the **US's formal response is still unknown**.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that a fifth of the world's seaborne oil and gas passes through, making it one of the most sensitive chokepoints in the global economy. Iran has periodically threatened to close or restrict it during standoffs with the US and Israel, and tensions escalated further this year after Iranian strikes disabled tankers, including an LNG carrier, transiting the strait. Oman, a neutral Gulf state trusted by both Tehran and Washington, has spent over three weeks brokering a technical agreement on shipping routes, fees, and a joint monitoring center. On August 6, Iran said it had agreed shipping-route coordinates with Oman, but Washington rejected Iran's push to charge fees and restrict US- and Israeli-linked vessels.

thread.previously: On August 6 we reported Iran said it had agreed shipping-route coordinates with Oman through the Strait of Hormuz, but Washington rejected Iran's push to charge fees and restrict US/Israeli vessels — the core dispute over navigation control remained unresolved.
thread.changed: The joint Iran-Oman statement is now reported to be in its final drafting stage, with reporting suggesting the deal effectively concedes to Iran's terms — a shift from where talks stood a day earlier, though Washington's formal response is still unknown.
