stories.title: Flavio Briatore wants every single F1 weekend to have a Sprint race — doubling the calendar to '24 and 24'
stories.what_happened: Speaking on **The Race podcast**, Briatore argued that Formula 1 should abandon or drastically cut back traditional Friday practice sessions — which he says offer spectators nothing worth watching, since teams just tweak car settings repeatedly — and instead hold a **Sprint race at every single Grand Prix weekend**, expanding from 6 sprints to 24. He said the alternative should be scrapping free practice altogether if it isn't going to be made more compelling for fans. Liberty Media, which owns F1, is reported to be more cautiously eyeing an expansion to around **12 Sprint weekends** over the longer term, not the full 24 Briatore wants. No change to the 2026 calendar is currently planned.
key_points: **Flavio Briatore** (Alpine's executive advisor) proposed running a **Sprint race at all 24 Grands Prix**
That's up from the current **6 Sprint weekends** per season — a four-fold expansion
He argues **Friday practice sessions** give fans nothing worth watching
**Liberty Media** (F1's owner) reportedly favors a smaller expansion, to around **12 Sprint weekends**
**No change is planned for 2026** — this is a proposal, not a confirmed rule

depth.background: A **Sprint race** is a shorter, roughly 100km race held on Saturday that gives out its own points and sets part of Sunday's grid, layered on top of F1's usual qualifying-and-race weekend format. F1 introduced Sprints in 2021 to add action to what was traditionally a quieter Friday/Saturday, and currently runs them at **6 of the season's 24 rounds**. **Flavio Briatore** is a veteran F1 team boss (previously at Renault and Benetton) now serving as Alpine's executive advisor, known for blunt, attention-grabbing proposals about the sport's direction.

stories.title: George Russell is 'overthinking' his F1 title chase, says ex-engineer, as his deficit to teammate Antonelli balloons
stories.what_happened: Former F1 race engineer Rob Smedley said George Russell needs to rediscover his "flow state" in his 2026 title chase, arguing Russell is overthinking his approach and overdriving as a result, while Antonelli is "just doing it very, very naturally." After the first half of the season, **Antonelli leads with 219 points**, Hamilton is second with 169, and Russell third with 160. Russell had briefly cut his deficit to Antonelli to just 25 points over three strong rounds, but then dropped 50 points behind after his race at **Spa-Francorchamps** ended after just five corners when he collided with teammate Hamilton. Russell has pointed to weekend-long power issues on his car as a factor that left him more exposed to such incidents, rather than attributing it purely to his own driving.
key_points: Former F1 race engineer **Rob Smedley** says Russell is **'overthinking'** his title bid and needs to find his **'flow state'** again.
Mercedes teenager **Kimi Antonelli leads the championship with 219 points**; seven-time champion **Lewis Hamilton is 2nd with 169**; **Russell is 3rd with 160**.
Russell had cut his deficit to Antonelli to just **25 points** over three rounds — then fell **50 points behind** after a first-lap crash at **Spa-Francorchamps**.
His race at Spa lasted **just five corners** before colliding with teammate **Hamilton**.
Russell says he's faced **weekend-long power issues** on his car that left him more exposed to incidents.

depth.background: George Russell is a Mercedes driver long seen as the team's likely long-term leader — but in 2026 he's found himself chasing his own much younger teammate, 19-year-old Kimi Antonelli, for the championship, while seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton (also now at Mercedes) sits between them in the standings. The unusual dynamic of three title-calibre drivers in one team has intensified scrutiny of Russell's form specifically, since Antonelli's rapid rise has made Russell look like the underperformer by comparison. Analysts and former engineers have started publicly debating whether Russell's struggles are mental (overthinking, pressing too hard) or mechanical (genuine car problems).

stories.title: Sergio Perez names the real reason new team Cadillac can't close the gap in its debut F1 season
stories.what_happened: Sergio Perez explained that Cadillac's struggles to close the performance gap in its first F1 season come down to **'a little bit of inefficiency and obviously a lack of development because a lot of it is done through third parties, so we don't control much of it.'** Despite continuous car updates, including a significant upgrade introduced in Austria, Cadillac's roughly **2.5-second gap** to the front of the grid has stayed essentially unchanged — the upgrades haven't moved the needle the way rivals' updates have. The team's challenge is compounded by timing: it's a new team debuting at the start of a brand-new technical rules cycle, which rewards teams with fast, in-house development loops. Perez said team principal Graeme Lowdon's squad is targeting more upgrades in the second half of 2026, aiming to be better positioned for its second season in 2027.
key_points: Perez points to **'inefficiency'** and a reliance on **third parties** for much of Cadillac's car development
The team's gap to the front has stayed around **2.5 seconds** despite repeated upgrades
Cadillac is F1's newest team, making its **debut in the 2026 season** alongside a brand-new rules era
Perez says the team is targeting **more upgrades in the second half of 2026** to set up a stronger 2027
Rival Aston Martin has already **leapfrogged Cadillac** with its own B-spec upgrade

depth.background: Cadillac joined the Formula 1 grid in 2026 as the sport's 11th team, fielding Sergio Perez — a five-time Grand Prix winner previously at Red Bull — alongside Valtteri Bottas. Starting a brand-new F1 team from scratch is notoriously hard: unlike established outfits, a new entrant has no legacy wind tunnel data, no long-standing supplier relationships, and often depends on outside partners for parts of its car design and manufacturing while it builds up its own infrastructure. That dependency is exactly what Perez is now flagging as the team's core problem.

stories.title: Franco Colapinto says Alpine hasn't even discussed his 2027 seat yet, as he hopes for an answer before the season ends
stories.what_happened: Ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix weekend, Franco Colapinto said Alpine has **not yet opened any discussion** with him about a contract for the 2027 season, telling reporters **'I haven't talked at all about next year, I'm focused only on going race by race.'** He said he hopes the team communicates its decision on his future **before the season ends**, rather than leaving it until the final races. Colapinto is having his **strongest F1 season to date**, with 18 championship points and a best finish of 6th in Canada, at times matching or outperforming more experienced teammate Gasly.
key_points: Colapinto says there have been **'no conversations'** with Alpine about a 2027 contract.
He's scored **18 points** so far in 2026 — his **best F1 season** — including a **6th place** in Canada.
He hopes the team decides his future **before the championship ends**, saying 'I hope I don't have to wait.'
Colapinto has regularly **matched or beaten teammate Pierre Gasly** on pace this year.
Alpine must choose between Colapinto and **other candidates** for its second seat next season.

depth.background: Franco Colapinto is an Argentine driver who joined Alpine's F1 lineup after impressing as a stand-in for Williams in 2024. He's spent this year trying to prove himself as a long-term option alongside teammate Pierre Gasly, in a competitive midfield battle where a team's driver choices for the following season are usually signaled well before the year is out.

stories.title: Europe's brutal heatwave sets off wildfires in Greece and France and pushes the Danube toward crisis lows
stories.what_happened: Firefighters are battling a wildfire in **Western Attica**, near Athens, that has been burning since **late July**, deploying more than 500 personnel and multiple helicopters; the effort took a tragic turn when **two helicopter crew members died** in a mid-air collision during water-dropping operations, and the fire has since jumped containment lines. In the UK, the Met Office confirmed **the driest July in almost two centuries**, deepening drought conditions. France has largely contained blazes in the Var region after weeks of fighting them, though officials warn strong winds can still cause flare-ups. Separately, the **Danube's water level has dropped to historic lows**, and Hungary came close to having to shut down its sole nuclear plant because there wasn't enough river water available for cooling — a step regulators try hard to avoid since it would strain the country's power supply.
key_points: Greece is battling a major wildfire west of Athens that has burned for **over a week**, after **two firefighting helicopter crew members died in a mid-air collision** while dropping water on it.
The UK just recorded its **driest July in nearly 200 years**, while France has managed to stop the spread of blazes in the southeastern Var region after weeks of fighting fire.
The **Danube river has hit historic low levels**, and Hungary came close to a **forced shutdown of its only nuclear power plant** because there wasn't enough river water to cool it.
Europe is warming at **more than twice the global average** since the 1980s, according to the EU's Copernicus climate service.
Strong winds in France caused flames to spread **'faster than a galloping horse'**, according to firefighters on the ground.

depth.background: Europe has spent much of this summer under an extended heat dome — weeks of unusually hot, dry weather that dries out vegetation and turns it into wildfire fuel. Greece, southern France, and Spain deal with wildfires most summers, but the **combination of prolonged heat, drought, and strong winds** this year has made blazes harder to contain, forcing water-dropping aircraft and thousands of firefighters into action across multiple countries at once. The Danube and Rhine are major European rivers that power stations, farms, and shipping all depend on; when their water runs low, it doesn't just affect drinking water but also **electricity generation**, since nuclear and coal plants use river water for cooling.

stories.title: Kerala's monsoon death toll climbs to 20 as red alert hits eight districts and thousands shelter in relief camps
stories.what_happened: India's meteorological department issued a **red alert for eight Kerala districts today**, warning of continued heavy rainfall, as the state's rain-related death toll climbed to **20** over three days of monsoon fury. **Pathanamthitta and Kottayam** districts have been hit hardest, with flooding and landslides inundating homes and cutting off infrastructure. Authorities have moved roughly **7,700 people** into about **275 relief camps**, and **five dams** are now on red alert as reservoir levels rise. Educational institutions have been shut in **10 districts** as a precaution. In neighboring Karnataka, a separate landslide has killed **3 people**, bringing the combined death toll across the two states to at least **23**, with rescue and search operations continuing for people still missing.
key_points: Kerala's rain-related death toll has risen to **20** over the past three days, with search operations still underway for missing people.
A separate landslide in **Karnataka** killed **3 more**, taking the combined southern-India toll to at least **23**.
India's weather office has issued a **red alert in eight Kerala districts** today, with **Pathanamthitta and Kottayam** worst affected.
Nearly **7,700 people** have been moved into roughly **275 relief camps** across the state.
**Five dams** are on red alert and schools are shut in **10 districts** as rain continues.

depth.background: Kerala and coastal Karnataka have been under sustained monsoon pressure for days, with earlier reporting putting the combined toll at 11 in Kerala plus 3 in a Karnataka landslide. Heavy, continuous rain since has pushed the Kerala figure alone to 20, with authorities racing to evacuate low-lying and hillside areas before more landslides hit. Kerala's hilly terrain, saturated soil from repeated rain spells, and dense population near rivers and reservoirs make it especially exposed to compounding flood and landslide risk each monsoon season.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill dozens in Gaza as Hamas rejects Trump's disarmament deal terms
stories.what_happened: Israeli strikes over the weekend of August 1-2 killed at least **25 Palestinians** in Gaza, according to health officials there, including four people in a strike on Deir al-Balah and a family of three — a couple and their nine-year-old son — killed in a strike on a house in Mawasi. The strikes happened just days after Trump's July 30 announcement of the disarmament agreement, immediately raising doubts about whether the deal will hold. Hamas negotiator Ghazi Hamad told Al Jazeera the group will not disarm unless Israel first halts its attacks and withdraws troops from Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office says the opposite: Israeli forces will not withdraw from the current 'yellow line' — the internal buffer line Israeli troops hold inside Gaza — until Hamas is genuinely and fully disarmed. Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a hardliner in Netanyahu's coalition, called the entire disarmament plan 'unacceptable' on social media.
key_points: Israeli strikes over the weekend killed at least **25 people** in Gaza, including **four in Deir al-Balah** and a family of three — a couple and their **9-year-old son** — in Mawasi.
The strikes come days after President Trump's July 30 announcement of a **'historic agreement'** for Hamas to disarm as part of the ceasefire's second phase.
Hamas negotiator **Ghazi Hamad** says the group won't disarm until Israel **halts attacks and withdraws troops** — conditions Israel rejects.
Israel's government says it won't pull back from the **'yellow line'** it currently holds until Hamas is **fully disarmed** — a standoff with no clear resolution.
Israeli National Security Minister **Itamar Ben-Gvir** publicly called the disarmament plan **'unacceptable.'**

depth.background: In October 2025, Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, heavily brokered by the Trump administration, that halted the two-year Gaza war. On July 30, 2026, Trump announced what he called a historic follow-up agreement covering the ceasefire's harder second phase: disarming Hamas and other armed groups inside Gaza. That phase was always the deal's biggest test — Hamas has never previously agreed to give up its weapons, and Israel has said it won't fully withdraw its forces until that happens. The gap between what each side says the deal requires is now spilling into open conflict again.

stories.title: RBI set to hold interest rates steady on August 5 as it weighs Middle East oil risk against a stabilizing rupee
stories.what_happened: Indian stock markets have been trading with a cautious, positive bias ahead of the RBI's rate decision, due Wednesday, August 5. The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra, is expected by nearly the entire community of forecasters — 29 of 30 economists surveyed by Bloomberg — to keep the repo rate unchanged at **5.25%**. The case for holding: retail inflation was a moderate 4.38% in June, within the RBI's comfort zone, and roughly **$40 billion** in new foreign exchange inflows — thanks to India scrapping capital-gains tax on certain investments and offering attractive dollar-deposit schemes — have helped stabilize the rupee without the RBI needing to raise rates to defend it. The case for caution: the renewed Middle East conflict, including the Strait of Hormuz tensions and Iran standoff, has pushed oil prices higher, and the RBI wants to see whether that cost passes through into broader inflation before it commits to its next move.
key_points: The RBI's six-member Monetary Policy Committee, led by Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, is widely expected to hold its key repo rate at **5.25%** when it announces its decision on **Wednesday, August 5**.
**29 of 30 economists** surveyed by Bloomberg expect no change in rates.
Retail inflation was **4.38% in June**, still comfortably inside the RBI's tolerance band, but policymakers are watching for oil-driven price spillover.
The renewed Middle East conflict has pushed up energy costs, a key upside risk to inflation the RBI wants to see play out before moving rates either way.
**$40 billion** in fresh forex inflows — driven by a scrapped capital-gains tax and attractive dollar deposit schemes — have helped stabilize the rupee without needing a rate hike.

depth.background: India's central bank sets its benchmark 'repo rate' — the interest rate at which it lends to commercial banks — roughly every two months through its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a six-member panel that votes on the decision. The RBI balances two competing goals: keeping inflation low (its mandate is roughly 4%, with a 2-6% tolerance band) and supporting growth by keeping borrowing affordable. Since the Middle East conflict escalated, oil-importing India has faced higher energy import costs, historically one of the biggest inflation risks for the Indian economy given how much fuel and transport costs feed into broader prices.

stories.title: South Gujarat is under water: Valsad gets a metre of rain in 24 hours as NDRF scrambles
stories.what_happened: South Gujarat is facing a severe deluge, with **Valsad district recording over 100 centimetres of rainfall in a single 24-hour period** — an extreme, cloudburst-level total. The India Meteorological Department issued fresh **red alerts** for multiple districts as the rain intensified. Rivers are rising fast in **Navsari and Surat**, causing significant urban flooding in low-lying neighborhoods. State authorities have deployed the **National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)** for rescue operations, and local administrations shut schools and colleges as a precaution. Forecasters expect heavy rain to continue for roughly another 18 hours, with **Dang and Tapi districts under watch for landslides**.
key_points: **Valsad district** recorded over **100 centimetres of rain in just 24 hours**.
The **IMD issued fresh red alerts** across multiple South Gujarat districts as monsoon activity intensifies.
Rivers are rising in **Navsari and Surat**, triggering significant urban flooding in low-lying areas.
**NDRF teams deployed** for rescue operations; schools and colleges shut for safety.
Forecasters warn of **heavy rain for another 18 hours**, with landslide watches for Dang and Tapi.

depth.background: India's economy and daily life run on the **southwest monsoon**, the seasonal rains that arrive from June to September and deliver most of the country's annual rainfall. Gujarat had already reported **flooding deaths and evacuations in the last week of July/early August** as heavy rain battered the state. Early August is typically a peak-intensity stretch of the monsoon, and this year's rains have already triggered major flooding in Kerala, Assam, and now Gujarat.

stories.title: IMD issues red alert for Rajasthan as a deep depression triggers major flood risk across central and western India
stories.what_happened: The IMD issued a **red alert for East Rajasthan**, its highest warning level, forecasting heavy to very heavy rainfall in the state. **Orange alerts** — the second-highest level — are in effect for Gujarat, West Rajasthan, Uttarakhand and East Madhya Pradesh, while yellow alerts cover a wide swath of states including Bihar, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Jammu & Kashmir. The system driving this is a **deep depression** that crossed the Odisha coast and is now moving inland, pumping large volumes of moisture into central India. It is combining with a separate **western disturbance** — a weather system moving in from the west that typically affects the Himalayan region — currently active over Jammu and Kashmir. The combination of the two systems is expected to strengthen rainfall across central, northwestern and western India in the coming days. Delhi-NCR itself is under a yellow alert and is expected to see continued wet weather.
key_points: India's weather office issued a **red alert for East Rajasthan**, warning of **heavy to very heavy rainfall**.
**Orange alerts** are in place for Gujarat, West Rajasthan, Uttarakhand and East Madhya Pradesh.
The trigger is a **deep depression** that crossed the Odisha coast and is pumping moisture across central India.
It's interacting with a separate **western disturbance** over the Himalayas, a combination that intensifies rainfall.
**Delhi-NCR** is under a yellow alert, with wet weather expected to continue.

depth.background: India's monsoon season, which typically runs from June to September, delivers roughly **70% of the country's annual rainfall** and is critical for agriculture, drinking water and hydropower. The India Meteorological Department (**IMD**) issues color-coded alerts — yellow (be aware), orange (be prepared), red (take action) — based on expected rainfall intensity and flood risk in each state. This year's monsoon has already caused serious flooding elsewhere, including in Assam, where floods have killed dozens of people in recent weeks. A **deep depression** — a strong low-pressure weather system, one step below a cyclone in intensity — forming over the Bay of Bengal and moving inland is a classic trigger for widespread, intense monsoon rain across central India.

stories.title: Israel's security cabinet meets as a military rift over the West Bank widens and settlers torch more Palestinian property near Nablus
stories.what_happened: Early on August 4, Israeli settlers set fire to vehicles near the villages of **Talfit and Jalud**, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, the latest in a string of arson attacks since late July. Separately, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said a Palestinian was wounded by Israeli gunfire during an Israeli raid **east of Nablus** the same day. Israeli media also reported a **new internal dispute within the Israeli military** over how far to expand operations in the West Bank, without detailing which factions are on which side. Israel's security cabinet is scheduled to meet later today to discuss the fragile Gaza ceasefire alongside escalating tensions with Iran, putting West Bank policy on the agenda alongside two other live crises.
key_points: Israeli settlers set fire to vehicles in **Talfit and Jalud**, villages south of Nablus, in the early hours of **August 4**.
A Palestinian was wounded by Israeli gunfire during a separate raid **east of Nablus** the same day.
A **rift inside the Israeli military** has emerged over how far to expand West Bank operations.
Israel's **security cabinet** meets today to discuss both the Gaza ceasefire and rising tensions with Iran.
The UN has warned West Bank settler violence recently hit an **'all-time high.'**

depth.background: Violence in the occupied West Bank escalated sharply after a late-July firefight in the town of Tal, southwest of Nablus, that killed four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers — each side disputing the other's account. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a wide-scale military crackdown in response, with troops raiding towns and detaining hundreds of Palestinians, while Netanyahu said his government would accelerate legalizing existing and new Jewish settlement outposts in the West Bank. Israeli settlers have since carried out repeated arson attacks on Palestinian homes, vehicles and mosques across the region, which the United Nations says have pushed settler violence to record levels.

stories.title: Russia kills three, including two young girls, in guided-bomb strikes on Sumy — city declares a day of mourning
stories.what_happened: Russian aircraft dropped six guided bombs on Sumy in a 9-minute window overnight, with at least one bomb landing directly on a residential neighborhood. Rescue crews pulled the bodies of two young girls, ages 5 and 10, from the rubble of their home, along with a 76-year-old woman who also died. Four other residents — three women and a man — were injured. Beyond the homes destroyed, the strikes damaged an administrative building, a garage cooperative, and a building belonging to a children's and youth sports school. Local officials declared August 5 an official day of mourning across the Sumy community for those killed.
key_points: Six **guided aerial bombs** hit the Ukrainian city of Sumy between **02:08 and 02:17** on August 4
Killed: girls aged **5 and 10**, and a **76-year-old woman**; four more people wounded
Strikes destroyed **two residential buildings** and a children's and youth sports school
Sumy declared **August 5** a citywide **day of mourning** for the victims

depth.background: Sumy sits in northeastern Ukraine, just a short drive from the Russian border, which has made it one of the most frequently hit cities of the war — Russian forces have used the region as a staging ground for cross-border assaults and routinely target it with drones and aerial bombs. **Guided aerial bombs** (also called glide bombs) are old unguided bombs fitted with cheap wing kits and GPS guidance, dropped from jets that stay outside the range of most Ukrainian air defenses — making them hard and expensive to intercept even though the bombs themselves are cheap. The attack came in the same week Russia carried out its **biggest missile-and-drone barrage in weeks on Kyiv**, killing 17, showing the aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities has not slowed.

stories.title: Two firefighters die when a wall collapses while battling a blaze at a Greater Noida chip factory
stories.what_happened: Late on the night of **August 3**, a fire broke out at **ILGIM**, an electronics chip manufacturing company in the Ecotech-3 industrial area of Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh. At least **six fire brigade vehicles** were dispatched once the blaze was reported. While firefighters were working to put out the fire, a **wall and an iron beam inside the factory suddenly collapsed**, striking five of the firefighters. **Tirthpal Singh and Rohit Yadav died** in the collapse, while the other three injured personnel are in stable condition and being treated.
key_points: A fire broke out late Monday night at **ILGIM**, an electronics chip manufacturing unit in Greater Noida's **Ecotech-3 industrial area**.
A **wall and iron beam collapsed** on firefighters while they worked to douse the blaze, killing **2 and injuring 3 more**.
The two firefighters killed were identified as **Tirthpal Singh and Rohit Yadav**.
At least **six fire brigade vehicles** were rushed to the site once the blaze was reported.
The three injured firefighters are reported to be in **stable condition**.

depth.background: Greater Noida's **Ecotech-3** is a dense industrial zone housing electronics and manufacturing units on the outskirts of Delhi. Factory fires are a recurring hazard in India's rapidly built industrial parks, where structural safety standards and fire-response infrastructure can lag the pace of construction. Firefighters battling factory blazes routinely face risks beyond the fire itself, including structural collapse in buildings not designed to withstand prolonged heat and water exposure.

stories.title: The US is drafting a ban on Chinese-made AI data-center parts that Nvidia and Broadcom quietly depend on
stories.what_happened: Reuters reported on August 4 that the **FCC** is drafting a rule that would ban new-model imports of Chinese-made optical transceivers used in AI and cloud data centers. The two companies most exposed are **Zhongji Innolight** and **Eoptolink**, which together control more than 60% of the global market for the high-bandwidth 800G-and-above transceivers that power modern AI clusters, and which supply a majority of Nvidia's 800G module demand. Analysts at Counterpoint Research estimate Western manufacturers would need **12 to 24 months** to build enough capacity to replace that volume. Complicating any pivot, the leading Western alternative depends on **indium phosphide**, a substrate already under Chinese export licensing controls that pushed its price up roughly 250% in 2025. The rule remains in draft form, with the White House aiming to impose it sometime in 2026 and China saying it will respond if the ban proceeds; it would only affect new imports, leaving already-installed hardware untouched.
key_points: The **FCC** is drafting a rule to ban new imports of **Chinese-made optical transceivers** — the parts that shuttle data between AI servers at light speed.
Two Chinese firms, **Innolight and Eoptolink**, together supply over **60%** of the high-speed (800G+) transceivers used in AI data centers, including most of Nvidia's own module needs.
Western suppliers need an estimated **12 to 24 months** to ramp up replacement capacity, according to Counterpoint Research.
The alternative parts depend on **indium phosphide**, a material China already restricts — its price has jumped roughly **250%** since 2025.
The ban is still a draft with no set effective date, and wouldn't touch transceivers already installed in US data centers.

depth.background: Optical transceivers are the unglamorous plumbing of the AI boom — small modules that convert electrical signals to light so data can move between the tens of thousands of servers inside an AI data center fast enough to keep GPUs fed. As Washington has restricted the sale of advanced Nvidia chips *to* China, China's own suppliers have simultaneously become the dominant, low-cost source for this specific component *inside* American data centers — a dependency few outside the industry had noticed. The move fits a broader pattern of the Trump administration using national-security tools to squeeze Chinese suppliers out of the AI supply chain, following earlier restrictions on chipmaking equipment and rare-earth materials.

stories.title: FIA fires back at F1 manufacturers, says they blocked fixes to the widely-hated 2026 rules
stories.what_happened: Facing sustained criticism from drivers including Hamilton, Verstappen and Sainz, the FIA pushed back publicly, arguing it isn't at fault for failing to anticipate the 2026 rules' problems. Tombazis said the governing body knew the changes would be difficult for drivers to adapt to, but that its hands were tied on making adjustments ahead of the season because the power-unit manufacturers could not agree on rule tweaks in time. When Sainz's comments were put to Hamilton, the seven-time champion agreed, adding pointedly that whoever made the original decision on the rules 'still got their job.' The FIA says some easing has already happened through deployment-rule tweaks introduced at the Miami race, with bigger changes — including more combustion-engine output — planned for 2027 and 2028.
key_points: FIA single-seater director **Nikolas Tombazis** says the body knew the **2026 rules** would be tricky well in advance.
He says pre-season attempts to fix the problems were blocked because **power-unit manufacturers** couldn't agree.
Reacting to Carlos Sainz's criticism, Lewis Hamilton said whoever made the decision 'still got their job.'
Verstappen has likened racing under the new rules to '**Formula E on steroids**'; Alonso called it the 'battery world championship.'
Further fixes are planned for **2027 and 2028** with more combustion-engine power, after smaller tweaks already made at Miami.

depth.background: F1's 2026 season introduced a major regulation overhaul: new hybrid power units that lean much more heavily on electric battery power relative to the combustion engine, meant to make the sport greener and attract new manufacturers. In practice, drivers across the grid have complained the cars run out of usable electric power mid-corner, forcing them to slow down well before braking zones and creating awkward, 'yo-yo' overtaking moves that look unnatural on track. The backlash has been near-universal, intensifying after difficult races at classic circuits like Spa just before the summer break, and some pundits have warned the sport risks a 'NASCAR-style' loss of appeal if the format issues aren't fixed.

stories.title: Europe's heatwave is now an energy crisis too — Hungary's only nuclear plant is nearing a forced shutdown
stories.what_happened: A prolonged heatwave has pushed the Danube to record-low water levels, and Hungary's government says the country faces its **"most critical five days"** as the Paks nuclear plant edges toward what would be its **first-ever complete shutdown** in more than 40 years of operation. At the same time, wildfires fanned by strong winds have torn through **France, Spain, Italy and Greece**, forcing evacuations of hundreds of thousands of people. Spain alone has burned through more than **200,000 hectares** this summer — double its historical annual average — in one of its worst wildfire seasons in decades. Continent-wide, **1,254 separate fires** have burned over **250,000 hectares** since January. Temperatures in parts of North Africa are approaching **49°C**, and 2026 is tracking to be about **1.51°C** warmer than pre-industrial times, which would make it the second-warmest year ever measured.
key_points: Hungary calls it its **"most critical five days"** as record-low Danube water levels threaten to force a first-ever full shutdown of its **sole nuclear plant**.
Spain has burned over **200,000 hectares** this summer — **twice** its historical yearly average.
Across Europe, **1,254 fires** have burned more than **250,000 hectares** since the start of 2026.
Hundreds of thousands evacuated across **France, Italy and Spain** as wildfires spread with strong winds.
2026 is on track to be roughly **1.51°C** above pre-industrial levels — potentially the **second-warmest year on record**.

depth.background: Nuclear reactors need constant river or sea water to cool their cores; when a river runs too low or too warm, plants must throttle down or shut off entirely to avoid overheating. Hungary's **Paks nuclear plant** supplies a large share of the country's electricity and depends on the **Danube** for cooling water. Europe has now had several consecutive summers of intensifying heat and drought, each one testing energy and water infrastructure that wasn't originally built for this level of stress.

stories.title: Mick Schumacher says he now wants to stay in IndyCar through 2027, as his F1 comeback hopes fade
stories.what_happened: Mick Schumacher has said he now wants to **remain in IndyCar for the 2027 season**, having begun his rookie 2026 IndyCar campaign with Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing still holding out hope of eventually returning to Formula 1. That F1 hope took its biggest hit when Cadillac, the sport's newest team, picked **Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas** over him for its debut lineup. Since moving to IndyCar, Schumacher has recorded his **first top-ten finish** of the season at Nashville, and has said he is now **'100 percent' dedicated** to his IndyCar career. He has stopped short of ruling out F1 entirely, saying he **'wouldn't say no'** if a genuine opportunity appeared, but acknowledges a return is now a distant prospect.
key_points: **Mick Schumacher**, son of seven-time champion Michael Schumacher, says he wants to **remain in IndyCar for the 2027 season**.
He joined **Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing** in IndyCar for 2026 after failing to land another F1 seat when he left Haas.
His best chance at an F1 return — a seat with new team **Cadillac** — went instead to **Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas**.
He's already scored his **first top-ten finish** of the season, at Nashville.
He still says he **'wouldn't say no'** to an F1 return if a real opportunity arose, but admits it's now unlikely.

depth.background: Mick Schumacher raced for Haas in F1 from 2021-2022 but lost his seat and spent recent years as a reserve driver without a race seat, fueling years of on-again, off-again comeback speculation. When new F1 team **Cadillac** was building its inaugural 2026 driver lineup, Schumacher was seen as a leading candidate, but the team instead chose experienced drivers **Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas**. With no other F1 seat materializing, Schumacher moved to **IndyCar**, American open-wheel racing's top series, for the 2026 season — a switch that historically has made a return to F1 very rare.

stories.title: Women's Asia Cup 2026 dates confirmed: eight teams head to the UAE from August 28
stories.what_happened: Organizers confirmed the **Women's Asia Cup 2026** will be played from **August 28 to September 13** in the **UAE**, with **eight teams** taking part: **India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal, Malaysia, Thailand**, and hosts **UAE**. **Sri Lanka** go in as the **defending champions** from the previous edition. The announcement gives teams roughly three weeks to finalize squads and preparation, with India's women's side coming off a period of strong form that included a landmark Test victory at Lord's.
key_points: The **Women's Asia Cup 2026** will run from **August 28 to September 13** in the **UAE**.
Eight teams confirmed: **India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal, Malaysia, Thailand and hosts UAE**.
**Sri Lanka enter as defending champions**.
It comes just weeks after India's team made headlines with a landmark **Test win at Lord's**.

depth.background: The **Asia Cup** is the region's premier multi-team cricket tournament, run by the **Asian Cricket Council**, and the women's edition has grown into a key build-up event for the continent's cricketing calendar. Sri Lanka won the last edition, and India-Pakistan matchups in the tournament typically draw the biggest audiences given the two countries' cricketing rivalry. Hosting shifts periodically between countries; the UAE has become a frequent neutral venue for tournaments involving India and Pakistan.

stories.title: A Greek-owned bulker is hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, one crew member missing as fire breaks out
stories.what_happened: At around **22:00 UTC on August 3**, the crew of the **Minoan Pioneer** — a 93,283-tonne bulk carrier owned by Greece's Siena Seas and managed by Modion Maritime Management — sent a distress call reporting they'd been hit by an unknown projectile roughly 20 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The strike hit the engine room, knocking out all power, and a fire broke out in the crew's accommodation block. The vessel's **third engineer is unaccounted for**; the rest of the crew abandoned ship and were awaiting rescue and firefighting assistance. No country or group has claimed the attack. It is the **fourth such incident close to the Musandam Peninsula in five days**, a stretch of coastline that had been considered a safer route than the main shipping lanes.
key_points: The **Minoan Pioneer**, a Liberian-flagged, Greek-owned bulk carrier, was struck by an **unidentified projectile** roughly **20 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman**.
The strike hit the **engine room**, causing a total power blackout, and a **fire spread into the crew's living quarters**.
The ship's **third engineer is missing**; the rest of the crew abandoned ship and are fighting the blaze with outside help.
It is the **4th maritime security incident** near Oman's Musandam Peninsula in just **five days**, and no group has claimed responsibility.
It comes hours after **Trump gave Iran a 'last chance'** to sign a deal or face strikes — showing the threat is already spilling onto commercial shipping.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil** passes through by tanker. Tensions over it have escalated for weeks as the US and Iran traded threats and Trump moved to blockade Iranian oil exports; several vessels have already been abandoned or attacked in the area this year. Iran had separately said a deal with Oman to open an alternate shipping route through Omani waters was in its 'final stages,' a sign both sides know how economically damaging a closed or contested Strait would be. This attack undercuts that diplomatic track by hitting a ship on the supposedly 'neutral' Omani coastal route.

thread.previously: Trump had threatened strikes aimed at Iran's leadership if it didn't sign a deal, while Iran said a shipping-route deal with Oman was in its 'final stages.'
thread.changed: A commercial ship has now actually been hit on the supposedly safe Omani route, with a crew member missing — the conflict has moved from threats to a real attack on shipping.

stories.title: Shafique and Babar Azam century stands haul Pakistan back into the 2nd Test after West Indies' 344
stories.what_happened: After Pakistan's bowlers dismissed West Indies for **344** — Justin Greaves (73) and Roston Chase (70) leading the recovery, with spinner **Sajid Khan** taking **4 for 85** — Pakistan's reply started shakily before Shafique and Babar Azam dug in. **Abdullah Shafique reached his sixth Test century (107 not out)**, while **Babar Azam batted to an unbeaten 86**, edging closer to what would be his first Test hundred in four years. Together they built an unbroken **168-run partnership** that carried Pakistan to **266 for 2** at the close of Day 2 — leaving them just **78 runs** behind West Indies' first-innings total with eight wickets still in hand, putting Pakistan firmly back in a series-deciding Test they needed to win.
key_points: West Indies were bowled out for **344** — Justin Greaves (73) and Roston Chase (70) top-scored.
Pakistan's **Sajid Khan** took 4/85 with spin to help wrap up the innings.
**Abdullah Shafique** made his **sixth Test century** (107 not out) opening the batting.
**Babar Azam** was unbeaten on **86**, closing in on his first Test century in four years.
Shafique and Babar's unbeaten **168-run stand** left Pakistan just **78 runs behind** at Day 2's close.

depth.background: This is the **second and final Test** of Pakistan's tour of the West Indies, played at Port of Spain's **Queen's Park Oval** — a series-decider after the first Test finished level. **Babar Azam**, Pakistan's long-time talisman and former captain, has endured a well-documented **four-year century drought** in Test cricket, making this innings a personal comeback story as much as a team one. **Abdullah Shafique** has quietly become Pakistan's most reliable opener over the same stretch.

thread.previously: We reported West Indies had recovered to 239/5 on Day 2 at Queen's Park Oval, with Justin Greaves anchoring the innings against dominant Pakistani spin bowling.
thread.changed: West Indies were eventually bowled out for 344 (Greaves 73, Roston Chase 70, Sajid Khan 4/85). In reply, Pakistan's openers turned the game around: Abdullah Shafique made a century and Babar Azam batted his way to 86 not out, an unbeaten 168-run stand that took Pakistan to 266/2 at Day 2's close — just 78 runs behind, with the series on the line.

stories.title: Wildfires destroy hundreds of homes and force 65,000 to evacuate near Spokane, Washington — with an arson arrest
stories.what_happened: Three wildfires broke out over the weekend around Spokane County and merged into what officials are calling the **Spokane Complex Fire**: the Old Trails Fire near Airway Heights, the Autumn Lane Fire near Five Mile Falls, and the Fairview Fire near Mead. Together they have burned more than **8,000 acres** and remain **completely uncontained**. Spokane County Fire District 3's chief said the Old Trails Fire alone destroyed **640 structures**, with the total across all three fires climbing past **700**. Roughly **65,000 to 67,000 residents** were placed under evacuation orders, and authorities say some may not be able to return for a week or more. On Monday night, the Spokane County Sheriff's Office arrested **Aaron Farinacci, 37**, as part of its investigation into how the Old Trails Fire — the most destructive of the three — started. No deaths or injuries have been confirmed so far.
key_points: Three fires — the **Old Trails**, Autumn Lane, and Fairview blazes, together called the **Spokane Complex Fire** — have burned over **8,000 acres** and are **0% contained**.
Roughly **700 structures** have been destroyed, most in the Old Trails Fire alone, and the toll is still climbing.
About **65,000 people** were ordered to evacuate; officials say it could be **weeks** before residents can return home.
Police arrested **37-year-old Aaron Farinacci** Monday night in connection with the most destructive of the three fires.
No deaths or injuries have been confirmed yet, but officials say the true scale won't be known until crews can safely assess the damage.

depth.background: Spokane sits in eastern Washington's dry pine forests, a landscape that has grown steadily more fire-prone as summers get hotter and drier — a pattern climate scientists link to a warming West. The fires started Saturday, August 1, and spread with unusual speed, fed by high winds and tinder-dry vegetation after a hot, dry summer. Washington state has increasingly dealt with destructive summer wildfires in recent years. Local and state fire crews, aided by mutual-aid agreements from neighboring states, mobilized quickly but were still overwhelmed by how fast the blazes moved.

stories.title: Welsh Fire chase down Southern Brave with five balls to spare in The Hundred
stories.what_happened: **Welsh Fire** beat **Southern Brave** by **6 wickets** at Sophia Gardens in Cardiff on **August 3**, with 5 balls to spare. Batting first, Southern Brave were restricted to **115 for 8** in their 100 balls. Welsh Fire chased the target down comfortably, reaching **116 for 4** off 95 balls to seal the win. The result strengthens Welsh Fire's position as the group stage of the 2026 competition heads into its final rounds. The Hundred's knockout stage follows shortly after, with the **Eliminator on August 14** between the second- and third-placed teams, and the **Final at Lord's on August 16**.
key_points: **Welsh Fire** beat **Southern Brave** by **6 wickets**, with 5 balls remaining, at Cardiff.
Southern Brave were restricted to **115/8** batting first.
Welsh Fire chased the target down, finishing on **116/4** off 95 balls.
The win keeps Welsh Fire firmly in contention as **The Hundred's** group stage nears its end.
The tournament's knockouts begin with the **Eliminator on August 14** and the **Final at Lord's on August 16**.

depth.background: **The Hundred** is England's 100-ball franchise cricket tournament, launched in 2021 to attract new fans with a shorter, simplified format than traditional T20 cricket. Eight city-based men's and women's teams compete each summer, with the top three finishers in the group stage advancing to the knockouts — the second- and third-placed teams play an eliminator, with the winner facing the top team in the final. **Welsh Fire**, based in Cardiff, and **Southern Brave** are two of the tournament's eight men's franchises.

stories.title: Trump gives Iran a 'last chance' to sign a deal — or face strikes aimed at 'decapitating' its leadership
stories.what_happened: Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump told reporters Iran has **one final opportunity** to reach a peace deal before the US resumes large-scale strikes — this time explicitly aimed at Iran's leadership, command infrastructure and critical facilities, not just military assets. He said Middle East allies had asked him to hold off on new airstrikes to give diplomacy 'one more shot,' and that any deal should move in two phases, starting with reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping. Trump insisted negotiations were **'going on right now,'** but Iran's government has publicly and repeatedly denied that any talks are actually taking place, instead saying it is negotiating only with Oman over how ships pass through the strait. The contradiction — Washington claiming active talks, Tehran denying them — is now in its second straight day.
key_points: Trump says Iran has **one last chance** to sign a peace deal before facing large-scale strikes.

The threatened strikes would target Iran's **leadership, command infrastructure, and key facilities** — the same 'decapitation' logic used in February's strike that killed Supreme Leader **Ali Khamenei**.
He wants a **two-phase deal**, starting with reopening the **Strait of Hormuz**, the oil chokepoint Iran has been targeting since late July.
Trump insists talks are happening **'right now'** — but Iran's government keeps publicly denying that any session is underway.
This is a sharp escalation from Sunday, when Trump had paused a planned attack, citing progress toward a deal.

depth.background: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran for months, a conflict that escalated in late July when Iran began targeting oil tankers to effectively choke off the **Strait of Hormuz** — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's daily oil supply passes through. In February 2026, a US strike codenamed Operation Epic Fury killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, a 'decapitation' strike against the regime's top leadership. Trump has repeatedly threatened to repeat that approach if Iran doesn't negotiate, while Gulf states have pushed hard for a diplomatic off-ramp instead.

thread.previously: We reported that Trump said direct US-Iran talks would begin Monday afternoon to nail down a deal on a 'total' reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to Iran's nuclear program — but Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson denied any immediate plan for talks, saying Tehran was negotiating only with Oman.
thread.changed: Trump has now escalated from announcing talks to issuing an explicit ultimatum: sign a deal or face strikes aimed at 'decapitating' Iran's leadership, echoing the February strike that killed Khamenei. Iran is still denying that real negotiations are underway.

stories.title: 25 Democratic-led states sue Trump over new tariffs, calling them a 'pretext' for taxes the Supreme Court already struck down
stories.what_happened: On **Monday, August 3**, a coalition of **25 states** — led by New York and including California, Illinois, Michigan and Pennsylvania — filed suit in the **US Court of International Trade**, arguing that tariffs the administration announced on **July 23** covering more than **80 countries** are illegal. The new tariffs, ranging from **10% to 12.5%**, were imposed using **Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1930**, a law that lets the president respond to specific unfair foreign trade practices, unlike the emergency law the Supreme Court had already struck down. The states argue the administration is simply using Section 301 as a substitute to reimpose the same sweeping, country-wide tariffs the courts already rejected, without doing the country-by-country investigations the law requires. Separately, the administration also invoked **Section 338** of a 1930 tariff law to hit Canada with **50% tariffs** on autos, alcohol and dairy, in a dispute over Canadian trade practices — a move that takes effect **August 19**. The lawsuit asks the court to block the new tariffs entirely and order refunds of duties already collected.
key_points: A coalition of **25 states** sued the Trump administration Monday over its latest round of tariffs.
The suit says the tariffs use **Section 301** as a workaround for tariffs the **Supreme Court already rejected**.
The rejected tariffs relied on the **IEEPA emergency law**, which the Court ruled doesn't let a president impose them.
This is the **third lawsuit** the same multi-state coalition has filed against Trump's tariffs since April 2025.
The states want the new tariffs blocked and **duties already paid refunded**.

depth.background: Since taking office, President Trump has used emergency and trade-law powers to impose sweeping tariffs — taxes on imported goods — on dozens of countries, arguing they protect American industry and jobs. A coalition of mostly Democratic-led states first sued in **April 2025**, arguing he had no legal authority to impose blanket tariffs using the **International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)**, a law meant for genuine national emergencies, not routine trade policy. In **February 2026**, the **US Supreme Court agreed**, ruling IEEPA does not give the president that power. Rather than drop the tariffs, the administration reissued similar ones in July using a different law — Section 301 of the Trade Act — which is what triggered this third lawsuit.

stories.title: Amazon becomes the 5th company ever to hit a $3 trillion market value, riding an AI-cloud earnings beat
stories.what_happened: Amazon shares hit an all-time high near **$285** on Monday, August 3, giving the company a market capitalization of roughly **$3.08 trillion** and making it the fifth company in history — after Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Alphabet — to cross that threshold. The rally followed Amazon's second-quarter earnings report, in which **AWS revenue grew 36.7% year-over-year**, its fastest expansion in 18 quarters, driven by surging demand for AI computing capacity. Amazon reported adjusted earnings per share of **$1.97** versus the $1.82 analysts expected, on revenue of **$200.61 billion** against a $196.47 billion estimate. The company is now projecting **$220 billion** in 2026 capital expenditure, up from its earlier $200 billion forecast, as it races to build out AI and data-center infrastructure. The stock's gains over Friday and Monday's sessions combined topped **20%**.
key_points: Amazon's stock closed up **4%** on Monday, pushing its market value to about **$3.08 trillion**.
It's only the **5th company** ever to cross $3 trillion, after Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia and Alphabet.
The stock's **two-session gain topped 20%**, following a ~15% jump on Friday after Q2 earnings.
Cloud unit **AWS grew revenue 36.7% year-over-year** — its fastest pace in 18 quarters.
Amazon now expects **$220 billion in capital spending** this year, up from a $200 billion forecast in February.

depth.background: Amazon started as an online bookseller in **1994** and has grown into one of the world's largest companies through e-commerce, cloud computing (AWS), advertising and logistics. AWS, launched in **2006**, is Amazon's most profitable division and effectively rents out computing power and storage to other businesses — including the AI boom's biggest players, who need vast server capacity to train and run AI models. The **$3 trillion market-cap club** is an informal but closely watched milestone reserved for the world's most valuable public companies.

stories.title: Sophie Devine ruled out of the rest of The Hundred with a calf injury; Georgia Wareham named new Welsh Fire captain
stories.what_happened: Devine picked up the calf injury while attempting a catch early in Birmingham Phoenix's run chase during Welsh Fire's defeat. Scans confirmed she will not be able to return this season, ending her Hundred campaign early. Welsh Fire responded by naming Australian leg-spinner Georgia Wareham as captain for the remainder of the competition and signed Ireland all-rounder Orla Prendergast — who has 47 ODI and 88 T20I caps — as Devine's replacement player.
key_points: **Sophie Devine** injured her calf attempting a catch in Welsh Fire's loss to **Birmingham Phoenix**
Ruled out for the **rest of the competition**
**Georgia Wareham**, Australia's leg-spinner, named the new **Welsh Fire captain**
Ireland all-rounder **Orla Prendergast** signed as her replacement player

depth.background: The Hundred is England's short-format franchise cricket competition, where each innings is 100 balls. Devine, New Zealand's veteran white-ball captain, has been a marquee overseas signing and captain for Welsh Fire Women. Losing a captain mid-tournament forces a team to reorganize leadership on short notice.

stories.title: Trump's own DOJ drops vandalism charges against 4 people accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial pool — and Trump is furious about it
stories.what_happened: Pirro's office filed a motion to dismiss the case against Hearn, stating that the damage was actually caused by a **botched sealant installation**, not deliberate vandalism. Since the previous Friday, her office had already dropped charges against three other defendants — **Justin Carreno, Sophie Dennison-Gibby, and Cameron Thiers**. The filing says the sealant began peeling almost immediately after the pool's renovation was completed, and that the Department of the Interior did not give prosecutors the full picture when the case was first built. President Trump publicly criticized Pirro over the decision, saying she **'choked'** and made a mistake, and insisting the pool damage was still the work of vandals.
key_points: US Attorney **Jeanine Pirro** moved to dismiss charges against Olympic canoeist **David Hearn** and 3 others
DOJ's own filing says the damage came from **'flawed installation'** by a contractor, not vandalism
Sealant lining the Reflecting Pool's bottom had **'almost immediately' started peeling** after a renovation
**President Trump** publicly said Pirro **'folded like an umbrella'** and insisted vandals were to blame
Interior Department gave **'less than fulsome information'** at the outset of the case, per the DOJ motion

depth.background: Several people, including former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, were charged this year with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial's Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC — a case the administration had held up as an example of cracking down on destruction of federal monuments. Jeanine Pirro, the Trump-appointed **US Attorney for the District of Columbia**, is the prosecutor who brought and is now unwinding the case. The pool had recently been renovated, and investigators have since found the sealant on its floor was already failing before any of the accused was even near it.

stories.title: India loses pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah for the entire Sri Lanka Test series with a knee injury
stories.what_happened: Bumrah sustained a **left knee injury** while fielding during the **second ODI against England** in Cardiff, and the discomfort forced him to sit out the series-deciding match at **Lord's**. He underwent assessment at the BCCI's **Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru on July 30**, where his fitness was measured at around **95%**, but the medical team determined he wasn't ready for the physical demands of Test cricket. Despite some discussion about him potentially joining the squad later for the **second Test in Colombo** if his recovery sped up, the **BCCI confirmed on Monday, August 3** that he will miss the series entirely, and uncapped pacer **Auqib Nabi** has been added to the squad as cover.
key_points: **Jasprit Bumrah** has been ruled out of India's **two-match Test series in Sri Lanka**, starting **August 15**, due to a **left knee injury**.
He was hurt while **fielding during the 2nd ODI against England** in Cardiff, and had already missed the series-deciding ODI at Lord's.
Bumrah was assessed at the **BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru on July 30**, and doctors decided not to rush his return.
Uncapped fast bowler **Auqib Nabi** has been named as his replacement in the squad.
There had been talk of Bumrah joining for the **second Test in Colombo** if he recovered faster, but the BCCI confirmed his recovery is taking longer than hoped.

depth.background: Jasprit Bumrah is India's **premier fast bowler** and has been managed carefully by the BCCI in recent years due to a history of back and workload-related issues, so any fresh injury draws close scrutiny. India is preparing for a **two-match Test series in Sri Lanka** as part of its build-up in the World Test Championship cycle, and losing its most important bowler is a significant blow to the squad's balance heading in.

stories.title: India's rupee grinds toward record lows as the RBI keeps selling dollars to defend it
stories.what_happened: The rupee was trading around **95.29 to the dollar** on August 3, down more than **8% over the past year**, even after a modest one-month recovery. Traders pointed to **continued RBI dollar-selling** to slow the decline, following what they described as aggressive intervention in the prior session. Market participants cautioned that further rupee strength could be capped if oil prices rebound amid the ongoing **US-Iran standoff**, since India imports the vast majority of the crude it consumes.
key_points: The rupee traded near **95.29 per dollar** on August 3 — down **over 8% in the past year**.
Traders say the **RBI intervened aggressively**, selling dollars to slow the currency's slide.
India's **forex reserves — the RBI's war chest** — have been falling as it defends the rupee.
The pressure is tied to **Trump's tariffs on Indian goods** and fears of rising oil prices from US-Iran tensions.
A weak rupee makes India's imports — especially **oil** — more expensive, feeding inflation.

depth.background: The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** doesn't fix the rupee's value, but it does step in — buying or selling dollars — to stop moves it sees as too sharp or disorderly. It has been under pressure for weeks: the US has layered fresh **tariffs on Indian exports** this year (part of a wider round of tariffs on dozens of countries), and Gulf tensions have kept a floor under oil prices, which matters hugely for India since it imports most of its crude.

stories.title: Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj wins its first big Bihar seat as bypoll results split three ways
stories.what_happened: Vote counting concluded on **August 3** for bypolls in three states. In Bihar's **Bankipur** constituency, Jan Suraaj's Prashant Kishor defeated BJP's Neeraj Kumar Sinha by more than **19,000 votes**, polling **63,203 votes** to Sinha's **44,250**, with RJD's Rekha Kumari trailing in third with about 14,000. In **Madhya Pradesh's Datia** seat, Congress won, and in **Gujarat's Manjalpur** seat, BJP retained control as expected. The Bankipur seat had fallen vacant after sitting BJP MLA and state party president Nitin Nabin was elected to the Rajya Sabha in April.
key_points: **Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj Party** won its first big electoral test, taking Bankipur in Patna.
Kishor beat BJP's Neeraj Kumar Sinha by more than **19,000 votes** (63,203 to 44,250).
RJD finished a distant **third** with around 14,000 votes — a blow to the opposition's Bihar strategy too.
**Congress won Datia** (Madhya Pradesh) and **BJP retained Manjalpur** (Gujarat) — no upsets there.
The seat opened up after BJP's state president **Nitin Nabin** vacated it to join the Rajya Sabha.

depth.background: **Jan Suraaj** ('Good Governance') is the political party launched by election strategist **Prashant Kishor** — the man who has advised winning campaigns for Congress, BJP, and several regional parties over the years — after he decided to build his own party in Bihar rather than keep working behind the scenes for others. Bankipur, a BJP stronghold in Patna represented by the party's own state president until he moved to the Rajya Sabha (parliament's upper house), was seen as a tough test: a symbolic win here for Jan Suraaj would signal it can actually convert Kishor's strategist fame into real votes, not just headlines.

thread.previously: We reported that vote counting was underway in three state assembly bypolls — Bankipur (Bihar), Datia (Madhya Pradesh), and Manjalpur (Gujarat) — with Prashant Kishor's new Jan Suraaj Party chasing its first big electoral win in Bankipur, a seat BJP had held.
thread.changed: The results are in: Jan Suraaj's Prashant Kishor won Bankipur decisively, defeating the BJP candidate by more than 19,000 votes — a landmark first major win for his two-year-old party. The other two seats split along expected lines: Congress won Datia in Madhya Pradesh, and BJP retained Manjalpur in Gujarat.

stories.title: Karnataka finally completes its Congress cabinet — with no woman minister and two resignations in protest
stories.what_happened: On Monday, **Governor Thaawarchand Gehlot** administered the oath of office to 19 new ministers at a ceremony at **Lok Bhavan in Bengaluru at 5 pm**. The Congress high command had actually cleared **20 names**, but Bhatkal MLA Mankal S Vaidya was dropped at the last minute to accommodate senior leader S S Mallikarjun, and MLC Gayathri Shanthegowda — the only woman on the list — was held back over a **pending Supreme Court-linked dispute over her own Council seat**, leaving the cabinet with no woman at all. The final lineup gives Lingayats and Vokkaligas 7 and 5 berths respectively, creates a first-ever slate of 7 SC ministers spanning different sub-categories, includes 3 ST ministers, and hands 3 Cabinet posts plus a top legislative post to Muslim leaders. Senior leaders including H K Patil, Dinesh Gundu Rao, Lakshmi Hebbalkar and N S Boseraju were **dropped from the ministry entirely**. Alongside the ministers, **GS Patil was named Assembly Speaker**, AS Ponnanna Deputy Speaker, and Saleem Ahmed Chairperson of the Legislative Council. Within hours, at least **two Congress MLAs resigned their party organisational posts** in protest at being excluded, and Shivakumar publicly promised disappointed MLAs "future chances."
key_points: **19 of 20 cleared MLAs** were sworn in as ministers, taking Chief Minister **DK Shivakumar's council to its full strength of 34**
The expansion came **nearly two months** after Shivakumar became CM under Congress's internal power-sharing deal with Siddaramaiah
The new council has **zero women ministers** — the one woman on the approved list was dropped over a pending legal case on her seat
Berths were split along caste lines: **7 Lingayat, 5 Vokkaliga, 7 Scheduled Caste and 3 Scheduled Tribe** ministers
**Two Congress MLAs resigned party posts** after being left out, and several senior leaders were dropped entirely

depth.background: Congress swept back to power in Karnataka in 2023 on the strength of an internal deal: **Siddaramaiah would be Chief Minister first**, and hand over to his rival **DK Shivakumar roughly halfway through the five-year term**. That handover happened on **June 3, 2026**, when Shivakumar was sworn in with just 13 ministers — a skeletal team meant to be a placeholder. Filling the remaining berths meant satisfying competing claims from Karnataka's powerful **Lingayat and Vokkaliga** communities, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe legislators, Muslim leaders, and MLAs from every region of the state, which is why the full expansion took two more months of negotiation.

stories.title: Rajya Sabha passes bill giving small businesses real teeth to force overdue payments — as opposition disrupts the House over Amit Shah
stories.what_happened: The Rajya Sabha passed the **MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026** by voice vote on Monday. The bill makes arbitral awards in favour of small businesses **enforceable as arrears of land revenue** and recognises them as legally binding debt under the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code**, giving suppliers a much faster route to actually collect what they're owed. Buyers who want to challenge an award in court must first **deposit 75% of the awarded amount**, and if their case is still pending after **six months**, courts can direct that **at least half the award be released** to the MSME supplier right away. States also get more flexibility in how they staff their Facilitation Councils, and the bill mandates that these councils be properly resourced and digitised so cases don't pile up. The bill's passage happened even as opposition MPs kept up **sustained sloganeering** in the House, demanding Home Minister **Amit Shah** explain the police crackdown — including use of pellet guns — on students protesting a NEET paper-leak issue at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on **July 20**, and address separate allegations of donation theft at the Ram temple in Ayodhya. TMC's Sagarika Ghose and Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge were among those demanding the Prime Minister and Home Minister address the House directly.
key_points: The **MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026** passed the Rajya Sabha by voice vote, targeting India's chronic **late-payment problem** for small firms
A buyer challenging an arbitration award must now **deposit 75% of the amount** before a court will even hear their appeal
If that appeal drags on **past six months**, courts can order **at least 50% of the award** paid to the small business immediately
Unpaid awards become recoverable like **arrears of land revenue** — the same fast-track tool used to collect unpaid tax
MSMEs contribute **over 31% of India's GDP** and employ close to **39 crore people**, according to government data cited by ministers

depth.background: India's Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006 already required large buyers to pay small suppliers within **45 days**, with unpaid disputes going to state-level **Facilitation Councils** for arbitration. In practice, buyers routinely dragged out that process for years by challenging awards in court, starving small businesses of cash they were legally owed. Union MSME Minister **Jitan Ram Manjhi** introduced this amendment bill in the Rajya Sabha on **July 29** specifically to close that loophole, calling it "the need of the present time." The bill passed today, during the Monsoon Session of Parliament.

stories.title: Kimi Antonelli builds a commanding 50-point championship lead as Verstappen can now formally trigger his Red Bull exit clause
stories.what_happened: After 11 rounds of the 2026 season, rookie Kimi Antonelli sits atop the F1 drivers' championship with **219 points**, a commanding **50-point lead** over second-placed Lewis Hamilton on 169, with George Russell third on 160. Antonelli's tally includes **six race wins and three further podiums**, a remarkable return for a driver in his first full F1 season. Meanwhile, Max Verstappen's underwhelming campaign at Red Bull means he has now missed the top-two standings threshold his contract required by the summer break, which formally activates an **exit clause** letting him leave the team for 2027 if he chooses. Verstappen's manager has publicly stated the four-time champion still intends to see out his Red Bull contract, despite persistent rumours linking him to Mercedes, McLaren, and even a reunion with designer Adrian Newey at Aston Martin.
key_points: Rookie **Kimi Antonelli** leads the F1 drivers' championship with **219 points** after 11 rounds.
He holds a **50-point lead** over Lewis Hamilton (169) and a bigger gap to George Russell (160).
Antonelli has taken **six grand prix wins and three podiums** in his debut season.
**Max Verstappen** can now formally trigger the exit clause in his Red Bull contract, after missing a top-two standings threshold by the summer break.
Verstappen's manager insists he still intends to **honor his Red Bull contract** despite the swirling exit rumours.

depth.background: Kimi Antonelli, a teenage Mercedes rookie, has had one of the most dominant debut seasons in modern F1 history, a stark contrast to Max Verstappen's uncharacteristically difficult campaign at Red Bull, the team he has won four consecutive world titles with. Verstappen's contract reportedly contains a **performance-linked exit clause** — a condition that lets him leave early if the team fails to keep him competitive for the title, specifically requiring a top-two standings position by the summer break to keep him bound to the deal. With Red Bull enduring what could be Verstappen's least competitive season since he joined the team, that clause has become the center of the sport's driver-market speculation this summer.

thread.previously: Reports said Verstappen-McLaren contract talks had reached 'closing stages' as his Red Bull exit clause was looming, following his uncompetitive season at Red Bull.
thread.changed: The clause has now formally activated after Verstappen missed the required top-two standings position by the summer break, and fresh standings data shows just how large the gap to championship leader Antonelli has grown, even as Verstappen's manager insists he intends to stay.
